The idea of putting any restrictions on the aceesf. of ladies to the terrace of the House of Commons has now, it is stated, been definitely abandon.d.t 1i general feeling in the liouse proved to be strongly against the proposal, and all that is likely to br done is to make further accommodation for the tea parties on the terrace, which will obviate the pr" sent crowding. The season is, hr,wever, getting over, and probably any importont alteration will be left until next session.

Miss Ethel Liggins, a pianist of ten years of age. has male a successful debut. Her programme con- Aged of no fewer than 20 pieces, all of which ha(i been committed to memory, among these being Beethoven's sonata Op. 14 No. 2, Mozart's fantasia in C minor, and examples of Bach, Mendelssohn, Chopin, Schubert, and Moszkowski. The littb, pianist fxhibited a crisp touch and a very even technique and got through her task in a manner which delighted her audience..

Lieutenant Eloff,who is President Kruger's grand- son, and who came over to be one of the witnesses in the Jameson trial with President Kruger's nep- hew is now in London enj,ying the delights of the season. Both young Boers are handsome, gentle- manly young fellows, standing about six feet high, straight and well proportioned. They speak English with a decided accent. They have evidently the acquaintance of a first-class tailor, and they do credit to his cut As far as externals go, they might be two young Officers of exceptionally fine physi- que, who had been brought up at Sendhurst, in- stead of Pretoria. There is one difference more 'n their favour. .They have an exquisite politeness, from which our officers might learn a great deal. The way in which they greet a person to whom they are introduced is quite a lesson in courtly grace. in a full and brilliant chamber, graced by the presence of many ladies, the House of Lords at length reversed its long series of decisions adverse to the claims of the Deceased Wife's Sister, the second reading of the Earl of Dunrayen's bill being rarried on Monday by a substantial majority of 29. Fourteen times since 1852 has this measure of jus- tice been rejected b 3. the Lords. Once, it was true —in 1883—the Earl of Dalhousie carried the second reading of his bill by a majority of 7, but it was thrown out on the third reading by a majority of 5. In ,1891 Lord Dunraven kik his bill by the narrow malority of 9 votes,but bow this is avenged. Th 4 Prince of Wales was present to support a bill in which he has ever manifested a lively interesr,and the Duke of York was with him. The Duke of Cambridge was present,but left before the division, and the Duke ot Conmught arrived too late to take part. in it The Prince of Wales was marked in his congratulations to Lord Dunraven, and he himself held something like. a levee after the Lord Chancel- lor had left the woolsack, many peers offering their felicitations: Needless to say the bishops,who had attended in large numbers, did not take part in these subsequent proceedings. Unfortunately,with Parliamentary business in its present stare, there is not the least chance of the Commons having an opportunity to complete the bill, which has been so repeatedly carried in the Lower ,House.

When Mr. ilalfour was sharply heckled by Mr. J. H.Dalziel about the intentions of the Government. Mr. John Burns, in his blunt way,declared that the Elucation Bill was dead. The member for Batter-, sea was chided and ridiculed for Lis rash state- ment. Mr. Burns has now the laugh upon his critics. As a result ot Saturday's Cabinet Council, the Bill is dearl,slain by its own parents. Ministers like the Revolution, devour their own children.

The'first and most generally predominent feeling as to Mr. BaHones statement with regard to the abandonment of the Education Bill, even on the Government side of the House, was one of general relief that sneh an incubus should have been taken away. The Bill has been a nightmare to the Tories during the last fortnight, and they are only too glad to he rid of it. But together with that there is en undeniable feeling of shame and humiliation at the circumstances, and a growing feeling of resentment at the leadership which has led up to all this. The danger of the future for the Unionists lies in the beginning of recriminations. •If they once begin they will not stop. Mr. Barfeur is treated with a general lf-Yity, due to his great services to the party. But the grumbling has begun, and he -will not-survive another slip. He would-be a bold man who would say certainly that the Government would end the Session with Mr. Balfour as leader. Mr. Chamberlain waits for the reversion, end there are those who are beginning to look to him.

Mr. Balfour,has got into anpther hole—this time with a Pat is factory result. The Leader of the FTou played a golf mach with Mr. John Penn, M.P.. on Saturday at Honor Oak Golf Links. Mr. Penn i 4 mighty on the sward. but Mr. Balfour. after being three holes to the bad on the first, round, "made really brilliant display" in the second round, and won the match by one hole.

The news fro Bulawayo is of such a serious nature that the Government has given Sir Frederick Carrington authority to raise further volunteers fnr ssrvice in Matabeleland. Thaquickest way to reach F,-rt Salisbut is through 'Portuguese territory via Delagea Bay, and reinforcements are to be sent tip that way, the, Portuguese having' given permission Fort Salisbury's danger arises largely from the fact that Mr, Cecil Rhodes has taken all the available able-bohied men to Buluwaio, and these cannot re. trirn (pia enough to be a certain relief to the Fort. Still, a force is to be sent from that direction, and their places is to be taken at'Buluwayo by Colonel Plurner's briginal Imperial force, now at Nrafekiou• Sir Frederick Carrington's action in advising f• u b alterittihn* yid reinforcements show what a 'serious view he takes of the situation.

The latest move of President Kruger—or :rather, perhaps. of Dr. Leyds, whose implacable jealousy and'dislike•of England are Probably at the bottom of •the new despatch—is intended td corner, not Mr. Chamberlain merely, but the British Govern- ment itself. First among the restions which arise is how the demand happens to be published. PreAiden` Kruger adopted the new deplomseY ? Perhaps Mr. Chamberlain's &St knowledge of it derived from Reuter's telegram. Of course he will not complain if he is thus ,paid back in his own coin, hut the chief point is what reply he will re turn to the demand, or complaint, or inquiry, or who tever•the name should he which diplomacy to give it. At'present British diplomacy does not -appear to he in possession of the cyper has reed them in newspapers. and probably that all. Has President Kruger officially communicated to Afr/Chamherlain any informotion about the ex- i,:tence of such telegrams,: if not, what proof have theltritish Government of the implication of either Mr. Rhodes or Mr. Beit in the Transvaal raid? On the other hand, if the Transvaal Government lige, officially communicated theme the corner becomea difficult Otte for Mr. Chamberlain. Some member of the new Radical party 41 speedily give him an ,opportunity Qf saying how 11 e intends to get round it.

I find the Liberals were .on Wednesday night. greatly Plated over the effect of the debate on th. Rating- Bill: They declare,and not withinit•reason. That Mr. Chaplin was utterlyunable to reply to th., arguments brought forward on behalf of the differ ent amendments; and thaCthe—whole diacus.iot ha'lt, damaging effect uponille Government. I ati told that at least'n dozn Unritinist mamberit were Jr the smoking-room during ...Wednesday's divisiorj? and absolutely refused to take part in them. It i- certainly very noteworthy that the Governmen• majority, which, owing to the absence of Iris' members, ow, h t to he aboutlBo, is now very after reduced to under 100. . „ .

: Thera is one .important member of the Cabine: whoshas never reconciled himself to , the abandon ment of the financial clauses of the Education Bill, and thicia Mr.:Chamberlatn. 3 ,hear on excellent authority that. even after the adjourned meeting of the Cabinet on Monday be declined to give up th, case as hopeless, and he secured an informal mew in Ql' his leading 'colleagues •after. the House bp, assembled to consider whether it WAR possible I. reverse the decision. arrived at. The fate of tit clauses WAR in the.balance up to the very monwrl when Mr. Balfour rose to make his statement; an even now there are leading members of the (3l,,ver, tnent who think that a mistake has been made it carrying over this question into another year an probably, doing a good deal to ruin ...anoth, f-ession. PREVIOUS. —Lawyer "You will get your thfrd out of the estate, madam." Widow " Oh, Mr. Bluebags ! How can you say such a thing, with my second hardly cold. in his grave ? " AN ANCIENT HousE.—llashaway : " I had no idea that your family was such an old one." Travers (proudly) : " I should say it was. Why, old man, we have some bills dating back four generations ! " A CULINARY GRADUATE.—Grandma: "And your mamma cooks nice things for dinner herself, does she? Aud does papa say grace when he sits down at table?" Tommy: "Well, he says Gracious I"'

THE GUEST CHAMBEE.—" So this beautifully- furnished room is your guest chamber?" remarked Mr. Heights, admiringly. "Yes," responded Mr. Isolite, of Lonesomehurst ; "that is whe.re our servant-girl sleeps, when we have cue." Mistress : " Bridget, how many policemen did you have in the kitchen last night?" Bridget (modestly).: " Only foive, mum." Mistress : "Couldn't you induce one of them to stay all night? You know I am afraid of burglars." Bridget (brightening) : " Rist. aisy, mum ; three av 'em shlapes here regular."

THE FAMILY MAN. He drives the nail in silence grim, But he is far from dumb. You know it by the sound from him . Each time he hits his thumb. LIKELY TO ItEMEMBER.—PIOI.Id .Mother: "You hven't kissed the baby." Bachelor Uncle: "Urn - try to remember next _time. "I'll kiss her when I—er—com m Europe." back from "When will that be "Let—me—see. About sixteen years." A DRAMATIC TRIUMPH AT LAST. Lobby- lounger : "how was the play last night ? " Firsniter : "Wonderful ! Most artistic and dra- matic production seen for years. Held the audience spellbound from first to last. Why, sir, in some of the thrilling situations there were times when not a sound could be heard but the hard bra_:athing of Othello, the suppressed sobs of Desde- mona, and the conversation in the boxes." "I AM very much better this morning," said Mrs. M'Bride. "I feel like a new woman." " I hope you won't dress like one," replied her hus- band, -fervently. A GENTLE SARCASM.—A Connecticut man once called at a farmhouse, and was asked by the farmer to take a glass of cider which he-had made from his own. apples. After drinking the cider, the man didn't exactly smack his lips, but turning to the farmer, said "Pity you hadn't another apple." " Why 2" asked the farmer. "Oh, you could have made another barrel of it!" was the answer.

ON THE WRONG TACK.—The villain gnashed his gleaming teeth with a grating sound. "Ha, ha! my proud beauty," he hissed, "I will yet bring you to the dust !" The proud beauty smiled a wan little smile. " Never," she twittered. " You are on the wrong tack. The man to win me must bring the dust to me." • . EASILY ANSWERED. —" Why," shouted the impassioned orator, "why is it that the wives of our farmers lack the happy, contented look to be found on the face of the bareheaded peasant. woman of the Continent ? " "Because," said the man near the door, "because the bareheaded peasant-woman does not have to worry all the time about her hat being on straight." NOT HER SPHERE.—Mrs. Cobwigger : "I don't see why I shouldn't be considered in regard to the new house we move into." Cobwigger : "Why, my dear, I don't see what difference it can make to you. Since you have joined all the women's clubs you are never at home." Summit: "Mr. Jagway called on me last night, and I think he had been drink- ing." Miss Pallisade : "He told me this morning that you looked beautiful." HOME TRAINING.—" Are you married" said the manager to a man who was looking for a situation. "No, sir." "Then I can't employ you. I have a place into which I could put you, but we engage only married men." "May I ask the reason of this discrimination? Is it .that families may be provided with support ! " "Not at all. It is because we find that married men know better how to obey than bachelors." Miss Oetthere (enthusiastic worker at church bazaar) : "Now, Mr. Slimpurse, you really must take a chance in this beautiful pipe; you really must. Just think, the pipe is worth twenty

lings, and the chances are only one shilling each. Mr. Slimpurse‘.(edging off) : Very sorry, miss, but I don't smoke." Miss Gettliere: "Oh, but you can learn, you know:" Arr. Slimpurse : "Tobacco does not agree,with me. I would have no earthly use for a pipe." Miss Getthere (struck with a bright idea) : ""Well, there isn't the slightest probability of your drawing . ,it, you know."

" THERE was quite a fight in front of our place to-day," said a business man at the supper table. "Two men got into a row, one struck the other, and then the 'crowd gatheied: The man who was struck ran aml. Obbed an .ugly-looking stick, and rushedbba&liis eles blazing.' -I thought sure he'd knock the other man's brains 0..1,, and I stepped. right in between them." The young heir had

gfen over eating his tart as the nar'i•ative pro- ceeded, and his eyes leaned right out of his head. was preudief his father's valour and he tried— couldn'L. knock any brains dui of you, could he, father?" The father looked long and curiously at his son and heir, but the lad's countenance was frank and innocent and open. When it closed *ith the tart on the inside the father gasped slightly and resumed his supper. Too GOOD A FeaLow-.—Years ago there was a very queer old clergyman in the diocese of Canter- bury, of whom a hundred anecdotes are told. 'On his going one day to order a wig, the barber, young in businesS, readily- accepted the order, and then ventured to ask his guest to dine. The invitation was accepted, and a bowl of punch followed, to which the divine did full justice. After it was over, the barber was beginning to measure, but his customer shook his head. m," he said, "you sha'n't make the wig." 'Why not?" exclaimed the astonished host. "Have I done anything to offend you?" "Quite the contrary; 3rou're such a good fellow that I haven't got the heart take you in. I'll go to somebody eke. You kiwi!, if you'd made the wig, you'd never have been paid for it !"- - WANTED A GRAPHIC ACCOUNT. —A short time ago the assistant at a railway bookstall in -a large city was surprised by a gentleman who rushed • ela to the platfaini and breathlessly asked for M.: paper with the mast graphic aceourit of the, China and Japan war. --The- assistant, noticing the excited and nervous condition of his customer, immediately complied with his request to the best of his ability. The stranger, sharply turning over the leaysohs purchase, gasped— "Ah ! I've got it at last:"(- The itian43f " *pedals," wishing to know the cause of his trouble, asked— "Have you any friendss or relations engaged in the war ?" "Oh, no!" said the stranger. "I'm a grocer; I'm in search of -a. naine,for our new blend of tea at one-andtaix.". A - you. remember I have frequently said to you that I believed Brother Meeks, who lives out -beyond South Squarn, came the nearest to being wholly sanctified of any oimY parishioners?" remarked theßeverend Mr. Lank; of the Hawbuck circuit; 'tot his wife,:soon after re- turning from a visit to that portion of his charge. "Well, now I grie-Ve to say that I entertain a grave suspicion of the genuineness of his sanctfica• tion." "Why so?" questioned Mrs. Lank& I spent the afternoon at the home of the Meeks family yesterday," returned the good man, "and during my stay -a severe thuderstorea caine up, and the house was struck by lighf• ning. Sister Meeks . had just . directed her has4ani4(totreltindle the kitchen fire preparatory to cooking Supper, and lie was dawn on his knees before the stove, blowing the coals vigorously, when there came a terrific clap of thunder, and a bolt of lightning came down the chimney and knocke4 him senseless. It also tore off nehtly all his clothing, scorched his-whiskers; and 13M-ted it streak down his breast and one leg_that looked as if done with a red-hot poker. It was sonic time before he recovered his senses, and when he did so all he said was to reproachiplly retnark .to his wife: 'Sarah, you oughtn't to treat me this way before the minis- ter,_ I was hurrying just as fast as I could.' I may be doing Brother Meeks an injustice, but I cannot help thinking that he is more hen-peeked ;than sanctified."

!ordefir and a written pspsr, and had left the office, and the magistrate was alone, before she walked up to the desk and stood before him. "Well, well,, young woman! Well, well, what do you want ? ' inquired the old gentleman, impatiently looking up from folding his papers. "I have come to give myself up for shooting Craven be Noir, who slandered me," answered 1 Oapitola, quietly. The old man let fall his handfuls of papers, raised us head and stared at her over the tops of his green spectacles. "What did you say, young woman?" he asked in the tone of one who doubted his own ears. : "I say that I have forestalled an arrest by coming here to give myself up for the shooting of a dastard 1 who slandered, insulted, and refused to give me sati faction," answered Cs titola, very distinctly. "Arn I awake? Do I htar aright? Do you mean to say tha you have killed a man?" asked the dis- mayed magietrate. `• Oh 1 I can't say as to the killing! I shot him off hi- horse, and then sent Mr. Merry and his men to pick him up, while I came here to answer for my's, If 1 '' " Unfortunate girl! and how can you answer for such a creatiful deed I" exclaimed the utterly con- founded magistrate. "On, as to the dreadfulness of the deed, that depends on circumstances." said Cap, "arid I can answer for it very well. He made addresses to me; I refused him. He slandered me; I challenged him. He insulted rue; I shot him." "Miserable young woman, if this be proved true, I shall have to commit you!" "Just as you please,'' said Cap, "but bless yoar soul, that won't help Craven be Noir a single bill" As she seeks, several persons entered the office in a state of high excitement—all talking at once, saying: " That is the i in 1" "Yes, that is eer 1" "Sae is Misa B ack, old Warfield's neice." "Yes, he said she was," etc., etc., etc. " What is all this, neighbours, what is all this r irvired the troubled magistrate, rising in his place. "Why, sir, there's been a gentleman, Mr. Craven be Noir, shot. He has been taken to the Antlers, where he lies in articulus mortis, and we wish him to to c mfionted with Miss Capitola Black, the young woman here present, that he may identify her, whom he accuses of having fired six charges into him, before Ms death. She needn't deny it, hecautai he is ready to swear to her!" said Mr. Merry, who constituted himself spokesman. "She accuses herself," said the magistrate in dismay. "Then, sir, had she not better be taken at once to the pre-ence of Mr. be Noir, who may not hase many minute* to live!' "Yee come along," said Cap. "I only gave my- self up to wait for this; and as he is already at hand, let's go and have it all over, for I have been riding about in this frosty morning air, for three hc,ura and 1 have got a good appetite, and I want to go hot! e to breakfast." "I am airaid, young woman, you will scarcely get home to breakfast this morning," said Mr. Merry. "We'll see that i rssently," answered Cap, com- posedly, as they all left the office, and crossed the strset to tbe Antlers. They were coneucted by the landlord to a chamber on the first floor, where upon a bed lay stretched, almost without breath or motion, the form of Craven be Noir. His face was stll covered with blood, that the bystanders had scrupulously refused to wash off, until the arrival of the magistrate. lint comp!exion as far as could be seen, was very pale. He was thoroughly pros- trated, if not actuatly dying. Ara und his bed were gathered the village doctor, the landlady, and several maidservants. "The squire has come, sir; are you able to speak to him 7" asked the landlord, approaching the bed. "Yes—let him swear me," feebly replied the wounded man, "and then send for a clergyman." The landlady immediately left to send for Mr. Goodwin, and the magistrate api roaohed the head of the bed, and speaking solemnly, exhorted the wounded man, as he exp :cted soon to give an account of the works done in his body, to speak the truth, the whole truth, and notaing but the truth, without reserve, malice or exaggeration, both as to the deed, and its provocation. "1 will, I will, for I have sent for a minis' er and I intend to try to make ray pace with Heaven," replied Le Noir. The magistrate then directed C p*.tola to coree and take tier stand at the foot of the oed where the wounded man, who was lying on his back, could see her without turning. C p came as she was commanded, and stood then with some irrepressible and incomprehensible mischief gleaming out from under her long es e- lashes and from thee .r.n: 1-s of her dimpled lips. The magistrate then administered the oath to Craven be Noir, and bade him look upon Capitols and give his evidence. • He did so, and under the terrors of a guilty con- science and of expected death, his evidence partook more of the nature of a confession than an accusa- tion. He testified that he had addressed Capitola, and had been rejected by her; then, under the influence of evil motives, he had circulated insinua- tions against her honour, which were utterly ut.justi- fiable by fact; she, seeming to have heard of them, took the strange course of challenging him—just as if she had been a man ; he could not of course meet a lady in a duel, but he had taken advantage of the technical phraseology of the challenged party, as to time, place, and weapons, to offer her a deep insult; then she had waylaid him on the highway, offered him his choice of a pair of revolvers, and told him, that having met, they should not part until one or the other fell from the horse; he had again laugh- ingly refused the encounter except upon the insult- ing terms he had before proposed ;—she had then thrown him one of the pistols, bidding him defend himself ;—he had laughingly passed her when she called him by name, he turned and she fired—six times in succession, and he fell. He knew no more until he was brought to his present room. He said in conclusion, he did not wish that the young girl should be prose- cuted, as she had only avenged her own honour; and that he hoped his death would be taken by her and her friends, as a sufficient expia- tion of his offences against her; and lastly, he requested that he might be left alone with the minister. "Bring that unhappy young woman over to my office, Ketcheni," said the magistrate, addressing himself to a constable. Then turning to the land- lord, he said: "Sir, it would be a charity in you to put a messenger on lalseback and send him to Hurricane Hall for Major Warfield, who will have to enter . into a recogthsauce for Miss Black's appearance at court." "Stop," said Cap, "don't be too certain of that! 'Be always sure you're right—then go ahead I' Is not anyone here cool enough to reflect that if I had fired six bullets at that man's forehead, and everyone had struck, I should have blown his head to the sky 7—Will not somebody at once wash his face and see how deep the wounds are?' The doctor who had been restrained by others now took a sponge and water and cleaned the face of Le Noir, which was found to be well peppered with split peas I Cap looked around, and seeing the astonished looks of the good people, buret into an irrepressible fit of laughter, saying, as soon as she got breath enough: "Upon my word, neighbours, you look more shocsed, if not actually more disappointed, to find that, after all, he is not killed, and there'll be no spectacle, than you did at first when you thought murder had been done." "Will you be good enough to explain this, young Woman 7" said the magistrate, severely. "Certainly, for your worship seems as much dig.. appointed as others I" said Cap. Then turning towards the group around the bed, she said: "You have heard Mr. Le Noir's 'last dy:ng speech and confession,' as he supposed it to be ; and you know the maddening provoca- tions that inflamed my temper against him. Last night, after having received' his insulting answer to my challenge, there was evil in my heart, Ido assure you! I possessed myself of my uncle's revolvers, and resolved to waylay him this morning, and force him to give me satisfaction, or if be refused—well, no matter! I tell you, there was danger in me I—But, before retiring to bed at night It is my habit to say my prayers; now the practice of prayer and the purpose of 'red-handed violence' cannot exist in the same person at the same time. I wouldn't sleep without praying, and I couldn't pray without giving up my thoughts of fatal vengeance upon Craven Le Noir. So at last I made up my mind to spire his life, and tei oh him a lesson. The next morning I drew the clarges of the revolvers, and re-loaded them with poor powder and dried peas. Everything else has happened j rat as he has told you. He has received no harm. except in being terribly frightened, and in having his beauty spoiled !—and as for that, didn't I offer him one of tne pistols, and expose my own face to similar damage 7—tor I d scorn to take advantage of anyone! ' said Cap, laughing. 1 graven Le Noir bad now raised himself up.in a

CHAPTER XLVII. CAPITOLA CAPS THE CLIMAX. "Oh! when she's angry, she is keen and shrewd; She was a vixen when she went to school; And though she is hut little she is £l.3ree." —SHAKESPEARE. It was qaAe late in the evening when Jein, hei messenger, returned. "Have you an answer?" she impetuously de- manded, rising to meet him as he entered. "Yes, miss, here it is," replied the boy, handing a neatly folded, highly perfumed little note. " Go," said Cap, curtly, as she received it. And when the boy had bowed and withdrawn, she threw herself into a chair, anti with little res- pect for the pretty device of the pierced heart with whiah the note was sealed, she tore it open and de- voured its c)ntents. Why did Capitola's cheeks and lips blanch, white as death? Why did her eyes contract and glitter like stilettos? Why was her breath drawn bard and laboriously through clenched teeth and livid lips? That note was couched in the most insulting terms. C ipitola's first impulse was to rend the paper to atoms and grind those atoms to powder beneath her heel. But a second iospiration changed her purpose. "No, no. no, I will not destroy you, precious little note 1 No legal document involving the ownership of the largest estate, no cherished love-letter filled with vows of undying affection, shall be more care- fully guarded 1 Next to my heart, shalt you lie. My shield and buckler, shall yen bet my sure defence and justificationl I know what to do with you, my precious little jewel! You are the warrant for the punishment of that man, signed by his own hand." And so saying Capitola carefully deposited the note in her bosom. Then she lighted her chamber lamp, and tak- ing it with her, went downstairs to her uncle's bedroom. Taking advantage of the time when she knew j he would be absorbed in a game of chess with ; John Stone, and she should be safe from interrup- tion for several hours if she wished, she went to ; Mayor Warfield's little armoury in the closet adjoin- ing his room, opened his pistol-case and took from I it a pair of revolvers, closed and locked the case, and withdrew and hid the key that they might not chance to be missed until she should have time to replace them. Then she hurried back into her own chamber, • locked the pistols up in her own drawer, and wearied out with so much excitement, prepared to go to rest. Here a grave and unexpected obstacle met her; she had always been accustomed to kneel and cffer up to Heaven her evening's tribute of praise and thanksgiving for the mercies of the day, and prayers for protection and blessing through the night. Now she knelt as usual, but thanksgiving and prayer seemed frozan on her lips. How could she praise or pray with such a purpose as she had in her he rt? For the first time Capitola doubted the perfect righteousness of that purpose which was of a - character to arrest. her prayers upon her lips. With a start of impatience and a heavy sigh, sho sprang up and hurried into bed. Sue did not sleep, but lay tossing from side to side In feverish ta.fitement the whole night—having, in fact, a terriole battle between her own fierce passians and her newly-awakened conscience. Nevertheless, she arose by daybreak in the morn- ing, dressed herself, went and unlocked her drawer. took out the pt-tols, carefully loaded them, and laid them down for service. Then she went downstairs, where the servants were only just beginning to stir, and sent for her groom, Jam, whom she ordered to saddle her pony, and also get a horse for himself, to attend her in a 'morning ride. After which she returned upstairs, put on her riding habit, and buckled around her waist a morocco belt, into w; ich she stuck the two revolvers. ; She then threw around her shoulders a shot Lar cape that concealed the weapons, and put on her lint and gloves and went below. Sha found her little groom already at the doer with the 'horses. She sprang into the saddle raid, bidding Jena follow her, took the road towards Tip Top. She knew that Mr. Le Noir was in the habit of riding to the villiage every morning, and she deter- mined to meet him. She knew, from the early hour of the day, that he ()Mild not possibly be ahead of her, and she rode on slowly to give him an oppor- , tur.ity tv ov.e.Llke her., ,Probably Craven Le Noir was later that morning than usual, for C p tola had reachid the entrance •of the -village beiore she heard the sound of his horse's feet approaching behind her. ; She did not wish that their reneontre should be in the streets of the village, so she instantly wheeled , her horse and galloped back to meet him. As both were riding at tall speed, they soon met. , Sue first drew rein, and, standing in his way accosted him with: -" Mr. Le Noir l'' "Your most obedient, Miss Black," he said, with a deep bow. happen;to be without father or brother to pro- tect me from affront, sir, and my uncle is an invalid veterah whom- I Will not trouble. I am, therefore, •underthenovelneceseity of fighting my own battles. Yeateroay. sir, I sent you a note demanding satis- faction for aleinotutalander you circulated against me. ; You replied by an insulting note. You do • not eecap3 putiishment so! Here are two pistols; , 134411 are loaded; take either one of them; for, sir, we have met, -and now we do not part until one of us falls from the horse 1" And so saying, ghat rode up .to him and offered 1.1.ta ehoicnof the pistols. •. .

•itughed—partly in . surprise and partly in admiration is he said, with seeming good humour: "Alias Black, you are a very charming young and_delightfully, original and piquant in all your ideas! but yoa Outrage all the laws that govern the duello. You know that, as the challenged party; I have the right to the choie of time, place and arms. I made that choice yesterday. I renew it to-day. .When you achede to the terms of the meeting, I shall ,endeavour to give you all, the satis- faction you demand. Good morning, Miss." And with a deep bow, even to the Saps of his saddle. he rode past her. "That base insult again 1" cried Capitola, with the blood rushing- to her face. Then lifting her voice,. she again accosted him: 'Mr. Noir 1" He ttirried, with a' smile. She threw omkof the pistols on the , ground near him, saying: • ! - "Take that up and defend yourself." He waved his hied in, negation, bowed, smiled, , and rode on. lan Nom!" she called in a peremptory tone. Once more be turned. She raised her pistol, took deliberate elm at his white foreheicl,-and fired - • ' Bing 1 bang bang! BANG 1 BANG! BANG I • limes without an instant's intermission, until her revolver was spent. When the smoke cleared away, a terrible vision met her eyes.' - ' It was Craven Le Noir with his face covered with blood, reeling in his saddle, from which he , soon dropped to the ground. ' In falling,- his foot remained -banging in the stirrup. The well-trained cavalry horse Stood perfectly still, though trembling in a panic of tern*: froth which he might at any moment start to run, dragging the helpless body after him. Capitols saw ,this danger, and not being cruel, she tempered justice with mercy; threw down her spent ; dismountedi from her horse; went up to the fritlOn man; disengaged hia toot from the stirrup;-&2d taking hold of his shoulders, tried with &libel, might to drag the still breathing form from the distt road where it lay in danger of being run over by waggons, Le the green bank where it might lie in comparative safety. But the heavy -form was too much for her single strength. And calling her terrified groom to waist her, they removed the body. • • Capitola then remounted her horse, and galloped rapidly Jot° the -village, 'and up to the "lathes' entrance" of the hoteliyhere after sending for the proprietor, she said I have just been-shooting Craven Le Noir for slandering see; he. lies by the roadside at the entrance of the village; you had better send some- body to pick him up.' " MisS 1.". cried the astounded inn-keeper. Capitola distinctly repeated- her words, and then leavingithenn-keeper, transfixed with consternation, she crossed the street' and entered a magistrate's office, where a little old gentleman, with a pair of green spectacles resting on his hooked nose, sat at a writing-table giving some directions to a constable, who was standing hat in hand before him. Ossitola waited until this functionary bad_ his

div.head: E 27.1596
div.p: sitting, posture, and was looking around with an ex.pression of countenance which was a blending of relief at this unexpected respite from the grave and intense mortification at finding him- self in the ridiculous positioo in which the address of Captoia and his own weak nerves, cowardice, and credulity had placed him. Cap went up to him and said, in a consoling voice : " Come 1 thank Heaven that you are not going to die this bout. I'm glad you repented and told the truth; and I hope you may live long enough to offer Heaven a truer repentance than that which is the mere effect of fright. For I tell you plainly that if it had not been for the grace of the Lord acting upon my heart last night, )our soul might have been in fiddles now." Craven Le Noir shut his eyes, groaned, and fell back overpowered by the refL "N mv, please your worship, may I go home 2" asked Cap, demurely popping down a mock courtesy to the magistrate. "Yes—go Igol go 1 go!" said that officer, with an expression as though he considered our Cap an Individual of the animal kingdom whom neither Buffon nor any other natural philosopher had ever classifhid, and who, as a creature of unknown habits, might sometimes be dangerous. Cap immediately availed herself of the permis- sion, and went out to look for her servant and horses. B it Jem, the first moment he had found himself unwatched, had put out as fast as he could fly to Hurricane Hall, to inform Major Warfield of what had occurred. And Capitola, after losing a great deal of time in looking for him, mounted her horse and was just about to start, when who should ride up in hot haste but Old Hurricane, attended by Wool. "Stop there 1" he shouted, as he saw Cap. She obeyed; and he sprung from his horse with the agility of youth, and helped her to descend from hers. Then drawing her arm within his own, he led her Into the parlour, and putting an unusual restraint upon himself, he ordered her to tell him all about the affair. Cap sat down and gave him the whole history from beginning to end. Old Hurricane could not sit still to hear. He strode up and down the room, striking his stick upon the floor, and uttering inarticulate sounds of rage and defiance. _
When Cap bad finished her story he suddenly stopped before her, brought down the point of his stick with a resounding thump upon the floor, and exclaimed :

_ " aimmy, you New York newsboy, will you never be a woman 7 Why the demon didn't you tell me, sirrah 7 / would have called the fellow out and chastised him to your heart's content. Hang it, Miss, answer me and say." "Because your are on the invalid list and I am in sound condition and capable of takisg my own part," said Cap. "Then, answer me this: while you were taking your own part, why the foul fiend didn't you pepper bim with something sharper than dried peas?" "I think he i (pita as severely punished in suffering from extreme terror and intense mortifi- cation and public ridicule," said Cap. "And now, uncle, I have not eaten a single blessed mouthful this morning, and I am hungry enough to eat up Gyp, or to satisfy Patty." Old Hurricane, permitting his excitement to sub- side in a few expiring grunts, rang the bell and gave orders for breakfast to be served. And after that meal was over, he set out with his niece for Hurricane Hall. _ _

And upon arriving at home, be addressed a letter to Mr. Le Noir, to the effect that as soon as the I,t - ter should have recovered from the effect of his fright and mortification, he, Majar Wurfield, slaDuid demand and expect satisfaction.

CHAPTER XLVIII. BLACK DONALD'S LAST ATTEMPT "Who can express the horror of that night, When darkness lent his robes to monster fear? And heaven's black mantle, banishing the light, Made everything iu fearful form appear."
-BIuNDON.
Let it not be supposed that Black DJnald had forgotten his promise to Colonel Le bioir, or wets indifferent to its performance. But many perilous failures had taught him caution.

He had watched and waylaid Capitola in her rides. But the girl seemed to bear a charmed safety; for never once had he c night sight of her except in company with her groom and with Craven Le Nair. Aid very soon by eaves-dropping on these occasions, he learned the seeret design of the son to forestall the father, and run off with the heiress. And as Blacl7. D mald did not foreFec what succecs Craven 1,3 .Noir might have with Cap,t,,la, he felt the more urgent necessity for prompt action on his own part. He might indeed have brought his men and attacked and overcome C.ipitola's attendants in open day; but the enterprise must needs have been attended with great b.oodshed and loss of life, which would have made a sensation in the neigh- bourhood, that Black Donald, in the present state of his fortunes, was by no means ambitious of daring. In a word, had such an alt of unparalleled violence been attempted, the better it succeoded the greater would have been the indignation of the people, and the whole country would probably have risen and armed themselves, and bunted the outlaws, as so many wild beasts, with horses and hounds.

Therefore Black Donald preferred quietly to abduct his victim, so as to leave no trace of her "taking off," but to allow it to be supposed that she had eloped. He resolved to undertake this adventure alone, though to himself personally this plan was even More dangerous than the other.

He determined to gain lccess to her chamber, secrete himself anywhere in the room (except under the bed, where his instincts informed him that Capitola every night looked), and when the house- bold should be buried in repoQe, steal out upon her, overpower, gay, and early her off, in the silence of the night, leaving no trace of his own presence behind.

By means of one of his men, who went about unsuspected among the negroes, buying up mats and baskets, that the latter were in the habit of making for sale, he learned that Capitols omnpied the same remote chamber in the oldest part of the Louse; but that a guest slept in the room next, and another in the one opposite hers. And that the Louse was besides full of visitors from the city, who had come down to spend the sporting season, and that they were hunting all day and carousing all night from one weees end to another. On hearing this, Black Donald quickly compre- hended that it was no time to attempt the abduc- &ion of the maiden with the least probability of success. All would be risked, and most probably lost in the endeavour. He resolved, therefore, to wait until the house should be clear of company, and the household fall2n into their accustomed carelessness and monotony. He had to wait much longer than he had reckoned upon—through October and through November, wmin he first heard of an 4 laughed over Cap's '•ou,1" with Craven Le Noir, and congratulited h ins,lf upon the fact that that rival was no longer to be feared. He had also to wait through two- thirds of the mouth of December because a party had c•aue down to enjoy a short sbason of fox- Lunt jug. Tney went away just before Christmas.
Avid then at last came Biack Donald's opportu- nity ! And a fine opportunity it Wati I Had Sttan buth•elf enviged to furnish him with one to order, it could not have been better!

The reader must know, that throughout Virginia the Christmas week, from the day after Christmas until the day after New Year, is the negroes' satern:llia I There are usually eight days of inces- sant dancing, feasting and frolicking from quarter to ql..:rter. and from barn to barn. Then the bai i, the tiddie and the "bones," are heard from in.reing talial night, and from night until morning. And nowhere wbs this annual octave of festivity be.l more sacred than at Hurricane Hall. It was the will of Major Warfield that they should have their full satisfaction out of their seven days' cairiv,i. He usually gave a dinner party on Cnrstruas day, after which his people were free mall the third of Jinuary. " Dertinty, mute!" he would say to Mrs. Condi- ment, "they wait on us fifty-one weeks in the Tear, and 'in, hard ii we can't wait on ourselves the fifty- si. C.,)IA I"

Small thanks to Old Hurricane for his self-denial I He did nothing for hitnself or others, and Mrs. Cdudithetit and Capitola had a hot time of ,t in serylug him. Mrs. Condiment had to do all the coaing ani hou,ework. And Cap had to perform cleßt ot the duic of I‘l4jr Warfield's valet. And was tile way in which Old Hurricane waited on 11.,1;18,-;11
1., :iappened, !herefore, that about the middle of the Corituris week, being Wedoey, the tweety- e4.:nti. of December, all the house-servants and falai labourers, frqui 4iurrfcauojfaU ient eff.

noay to a nano rrreaz-aown grven at a ran nve miles across the country. And Major Warfield, Mrs. Condiment and Capitola were the only living beings left in the old house that night. Black Donald, who had been prowling about the premises evening after evening, watching his oppor- tunity to effect his nefarious object, soon uiscovered the outward bound stampede of the negroes, and tho unprotected state in which the old house, for that night only, would be left. And he determined to take advantage of the circumstances to consum- mate his wicked purpose. In its then defenceless condition, he could easily have mustered his force and carried oil his prize without immediate personal risk. Bat, as we said before, he eschewed violence, as being likely to provoke after effects of a too fatal character. He resolved rather at once to risk his own personal safety in the quieter plan of abduction which he had formel

He determined that as soon as it should be dark, he would watch his opportunity to enter the house, steal to Cap's chamber, secrete himself in a closet, and when all should be quiet, "in the dead waste and middle of the nigni," he would come out. master her, stop her mouth, and carry her off. When it became quite dark he approached the house, and hid himself under the steps beneath the back door leading from the hall into the garden, to watch his opportunity of entering. Ho soon found that his entermse required great Faience as well as courage. He had to wait more than two hours before he heard the door unlocked and opened. He then peered out from his hiding-place, and saw Oid Hurricane taking his way out towards the garden. Now was his time to slip unperceived into the house. He stealthily came out of his hiding-place, crept up the portico stairs to the back door, noiselessly turned the latch, entered, and closed it behind him. He had just time to open a side door on his right hand, and conceal himself in a wood cloi•et under the stairs, when he heard the footsteps of Oid Hurricane returning. The old man came in, and Black Donald laughed •Zo himself to hear with what caution he locked, bolted and barred the doors to keep out house- breakers I
"Lb, old fellow! you are fasteninz the stable after the horse has been stolen 1" said Black DoLald to himself.

As soon as Old Hurricane had passed by the closet in which the outlaw was concealed, and had gone into the parlour, Black Donald determined to risk the ascent into Oapitola's chamber. From the description given by his men, who had once suc- ceeded in finding their way thither, he knew very well where to go. Noiselessly, therefore, he left his place of conceal- ment, and crept cut to reconnoitre the hall, which he found deserted.

Old Hurricane's shawl, hat and walking-stick were deposited in one corner. In case of being met on the way, he put the hat on his head, wrapped the shawl around his shoulders, and took the stick in his hand.

His forethought proved to be serviceable. He went through the hall and up the first flight of stairs without interruption; but on going along the hall of the second storey be met Mrs. Condiment coming out of Old Hurricane's room.
"Your slippers are on the hearth, your gown is at the fire and the water is boiling to make your punch, Major Warfield," said the old lady, in passing.
- " Unipb, umph, umph," grunted Black Donald, in reply. _ _

The housekeeper then bade him good-night, say- kig that she was going at once to her room. " Uroph 1" assented Black Donald. And so they parted and this peril was passed. Black Donald went up the second flight of stairs and then down a back passage and a narrow stair- case and along a corridor and through several untenanted rooms, and into another passage, and finally through a side door leading in Capitola's chamber.

Here he looked around for a safe hiding-place— there was a high bedstead curtained; two deep windows also curtained; two closets; a dressing bureau, workstand, washstand and two aim-chairs. The forethought of little Pitapat had caused her to kindle a fire on the hearth and place a waiter of. refreshments on the workstand, so as to make all comfortable before she had left with the other negroes to go to the banjo breakdown.

Among he edibles, Pitapat bad been careful to leave a small bottle of brandy, a pitcher of cream, a few eggs and some spice, saying to, herself, ..Long as it was Christmas times Bliss Catterpillar might want a sup of egg-nog- quiet to herself, jes as much as ole marse did his whiskey punch "—and never fancying that her young mistress would require a more delicate lunch than her old master.

Black Donald laughed as lie saw this outlay, and remarking that the young °cell rtnt of On chamber must have an ppti te at tier own, he put the neck of the brandy bottle to his lips and took what he called "a hearty swig."

Then vowing that Old Hurricane knew what good liquor was, he replaced the bottle and looked around to find the best place for his concealment. He soon determined to hide himself behind the thick folds of the window curtai nearest the door, so that immediately after the entrance of Capitol& he could glide to the dour, lock it, withdraw the key and have the girl at or ce in his power. He took a second "swig" at the brandy bottle, and then wont into his place of concealment to wait events.

The same hour Capitola was her uncle's partner in a prolonged game at chess. It was near eleven o'clock before C ip, heartily tired of the battle, permitted herself to be beaten in order to get to bed.

With a satisfied chuckle, Old Hurricane arose from his seat, lighted two bed-chamber lamps, gave one to Oapitola, took the other himself, and started off for his room, followed by Op ctA far as the head of the flight of stairs, where she bade him good- night.

She waited until she saw him enter his room, heard him lock his door on the inside, and throw himself down heavily into his arm-chair, and then she went on her own way. She hurried up the second flight of stairs, and along the narrow p Issages, empty rooms, steep steps, and dreary halls, until she reached the door of her dot mitory.
She turned the latch and entered the room
The first thing that met her eight was the waiter Of provisions upon the stand. And at this fresh instance of her little maid's forethought, she burst Into an uncontrollable fit of laughter.

She did not see a dark figure glide from behind the window curtains, steAl to the door, turn the lock and withdraw the key. But still retaining her prejml!ce t\gpiust the presence of food in her bed-chamber, she litsed up the waiter in both hands to carry it out iutn the passage, turned and stood face to face with—Buck Denaid
(To be continued.)

div.p: A MOST GRAPH° STORY.
IT IS TAKEN DIRECT FROM REAL LIFE.

The unwritten romances of life are more wonderful and far more interesting than the most vivid works of fietion. The one we aro about to relate occurred in real life, and is both interestine and instructiee. Mr. Jas. A. Joy's (Cigar Importer, c,f 63, Corporation- street, Manchester) own words. Fie said :—" About four years ago I had an attack of influer 23, which kept inc in bed four weeks. When I got up and about again I was very nervous ; could get no sleep, could not eat, and suffered with pains in the head and face, which al- most drove me mad. I got worse and werse.week after week. Of course I had medical advice and various kinds 54 medicine, from none of which I received any benefit. When things got to the worst, and everybody, including myself, had given up all hope, I met a friend whom I had not seen for some time, and seeing the con- dition I was in (I had lost four stone in weight), he said, Try Warner's Safe Cure.' I laughed at the idea. No patent medicines far me, thank you.' But he insisted, saying : 'Don't get cne bottle, and use it, and then say it is no good. Your cace is too serious for that. It has taken years to bring you to your present cordition, and you won't be cured in a week, but if you will eet bottle aFter bottle for a month, and take it as per instructions, and you do not find yoursalf a ell on the road to recovery at the end of that time, I will pay for all that you have taken, and stand a guinea si'k hat into the.hargain.' I yielded, got a large bottle, and rd l giously took eight dng a a day. When that was done I eat another, and followed suit. At the end of two wet kg I felt no better. though everyone else congratulated me upin the im- provement that had taken niece. This encouraged me to go on. which I did for about four months. At the eed of that time I was aft well as ever I had been in my life, gaining weight all the time. Since then I have never had a day's illness."
At the Old Bailey on ‘VeAnesday Charles Baker, a traveller, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for forging' a will,

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAREST NELLIE,

Some other €mment authority once observed that if you had a good hat and carried a good parasol you could pass yourself off as well dressed in a comparatively shabby gown. There are numberless pretty hats and one of them is made of leghorn with a ruche of tulle round the brim, wide band of black velvt round the crosA,n,- two white tips standing erect, at one side, and a group of roses beneath.

A vs y prr,f ty little toque is of fancy shot blue and ;4 reel.) straw, trimmed in front with three one of periwinkle-blue, one of white mfure,nd.andther of green velvet.' The brim. is, mi-nkled at the "edge, and on the left side is a white ostrich tip, and some delicate bird of paradise feat here, which are really prettier and more grace-. tel than aigrettes. •

A charming' shape for a girlish wearer is one ihat has a brim wide and rooping a little over the face; but slightly curved up at the sides and drooping again at the back, where it is, however, rather. narrower. Such a hat would be .particu- larly pretty in tan straw with clusters of roses, shading from palest pink to deep ‘erimson,_ under the raised brim at the sides, and folds and loops of shot pink and pale brown tulle or chiffon round the crown. In black straw, too, with trimmings of black chiffon, white satin ribbon, and black velvet roses with pale green centres, it would have a stylish, if quieter, appearance, or the shape might be copied in drawn black tulle or net, with bows of striped blue and white chird ribbon and clusters of blue forget-me-nots.

A pretty dress for a little girl is of hyacinth, blue nun's veiling, the skirt with a deep hem, lined with stiff muslin, and three tucks above' the rest of the skirt, without lining. The bodice is made on a fitted lining, cut in three parts, and little strap v of ecru insertion lace, fastened with small filigree buttons form the trimming. The waist and neck are finished with a deep blue ribbon, • and the tight sleeves fitted with a pouffe(' top, divided in two by a band of insertion. An exceedingly pretty blouse is made of dainty fronts, lace collars, and various other trifles which go faritoward.s making an effective toilette. At the top of the page on the left is a blouse of grass lawn, with raised white embroidered spots; the front is trimmed with a waterfall jabot of the same material, and this is edged . with white Vaienciennes lace, and a pretty little frill, also edged with lace turns out ot the collar. The sleeves are pointed at the wrist, and trimmed with two little lace frills. This pretty blouse is lined through with cambric.

Very stylish looking and comfortable velvet corsages, are being worn, usually with cloth skirts of the same colour, but very frequently with black ones. The word velveteen may very often be sulbstituted for velvet, but the fact remains that the portion of the bodice that has the most wear and tear is of plain good silk velvet, while fancy velveteens are used tor the sleeves, and very fre- quently replaced by silk or satin sleeves before the velvet portion is in the least clentodJ or shabby. The sleeves and vest of Paisley velveteen in which a pale tint of heliotrope is the prevailing colour. On each side of the vest is a shaped piece of jewelled embroidery worked in many coloured beads, silks, and tinsels on a cream cloth ground. Plain viulet ribbon is worn round the waist. The skirt sent home with this top Was violet satin:laced cloth. Nearly all the evening cloaks are in the Empire or Watteau styles, and they do not fit in at the waist. Costly brocades and soft satins are the most popular materials for these garments, and they are lined with shot silks ani satins of the ros. delicate description. Some very lovely opera. cloaks are made of accordion- pleated shot silks, with trimmings of lace and jewelled passementerie. Pretty opera capes for young girls are made of fine faced cloth, with chiffon ruches round the edges and at the neck.
Your loving JENNIE.
"WOMEN'S CHAT."

A considerable amount of nonsense has been written on the subject of the extra work which the Royal wedding is entailing on the Lord Chamberlain, but it is chiefly fiction ; for Lord Lathom's work is mainly of approval and suggestion. ,The real labour is under- taken by the Qaeen's Private Secretary and the Master of the Royal Household, who are acting in conjunction with the Comptroller of the Prince of Wales' El isehold, , and the Prince's Private Secretary. Ttle" officials have I to arrangif all the details of the fitting up of the chapel

div.head: TUE I_,'XAMINTEII, SATITPDAY. ,TUNE 27, 1816. BE C.ILREPTI WITH THAT LAMP I sincerely hope that Mrs. Filmer has abandoned the
div.p: TUE I_,'XAMINTEII, SATITPDAY. ,TUNE 27, 1816. BE C.ILREPTI WITH THAT LAMP I sincerely hope that Mrs. Filmer has abandoned the

for the ceremony, the ordering of the procession, the c preparing of the collation and all the practical husiness of the wedding. Sir Henry Evvart, the Grand Eq aerry, will also assist.for it is his affair to see that the carriages and horses are brought up to time. It is a well known fact that Her Majesty takes the greatest possible interest in the marriages of all t),,,r de scendants anti just now she is concerning, herself very much about her eldest great grandchild, Princess Feedore. The young. Princess who is also a niecs of the Empeiror William, is just seventeen, and it is rumoured that the Prince who has found favour in her eyes, is not in favour at the German Court a.rd the little matri- monial difficulty is altogether causing some anxiety to her grandmother, the Empress Frederick, and her great grandmother, the Queen. The number of Royal widows, now more or less in public view, is somewhat remarkable. First, of course, comes our own Queen, then there is the Einprese Frederick of Germany, Princess Henry of Bettenberg., and the Duchess of Albany. Upon the Continenb there are the two widowed Cleeens regenr,lMaria Christina of Spain, and Emma. ot Holland, the latter lady, by the way, ie a sister of our charming Duchess of Albany. Then there is the widowed Czarina, Maria Feodororna. Austrian royalty has twe widows, and besides the ex Empress Eeeelie, France has e: Duchess of Orleans, whom the Leeitimists rank as Queen Dowager. TIIP last public appearance of Sir Augustus Harris, whose early death we one and all deplore, was on the occasion of the brilliant reception he gave at nrury-lane to the Chambers of Commerce on the 12th of June. He then looked very far from well, and the next day has illness began. It has been said that Sir Augustus Harris was the first actor-manager who has borne a title, but this is not quite correct. He received his knighthood for civic reasons, and the real distinction of being the first theatrical knight rests with Sir Henry Irving. Mr. W. B. Burdett-Coutts,who has recently celebrated his birthday, is nearly forty years younger than his wife. His marriage with the Baroness took place in 1881, when dispite her age,which was closempen sS‘venty the bride was arrayed in white and the orthodox erange hlessotne. At one time it was thought the Emperer Napoleon was desirous of marryins her, at another time- she might have marriel the Duke of Wellieeton, and never did a woman exist who by rumour has been engaged to be married so often. The Baroness's marri- age, however, has turned out very well, and both in Stsatteh-strett and Holly Ledge no happier couple are to he found anywhere. 'the author of the" Heavenly Twins," Madame-Sarah Grand, for all her propagandism of the cult of the "New Woman," has a low, mnsical voice, arid spies, gentle manner. She is atsove the medium height, with a rather slim iigiire, her face is a pure oval, an shape, and is crowned with soft curly hair.. She has abroad intellec- tual brow, eyes deep grey and saddoeking, and a com- plexion: very delicately tinted. She is descended on both sides from artistic families and at the age of eleven wrote and composed a song. Lille one or two others of our feminine authors of fiction Madame Sarah Grand has been a great traveller. ' . One of the most promising of our women novelise i; Miss F. F. Mentresor, the author of two recently pub- lished novels "Into tha Highways and Fledees " and "The One That Looked' On." Mi;s Montres ,r's early days :were sweat in Kent, though she has lived in Lon- don the greater port of her life. He father was an admiral but came of a long line of soldiers. [Tor pater- nal grandfather Sir Thomas Montresor was distinguished for active service in the Army, and her brother was k9led while defending the guns of the Naval Brieade at Tamai. Four new colours have lately made their appearance. Apricot, a lovely shade of pinky yellow, which bids fair to be immensely popular among brunettes ; a new green for blondes, a tritest perfect shade, without a tinge of yellow or blue; mauve, deepening to violet; and nastur- tium, ranging from pale yellow to orange and red. ,It appears the very pal. shades of biscuit, silver blue and pearl grey, are not likely to be so immensely adopted as was supposed early in the season. The Ascot parasols, which I omitted to mention last week, were positive poems. Many were a)f rnee coloured silk to accompany neutral tinted gowns and rose hued 1 straw bonnets or hats, and some were of or, ttv pale rhino silks One I PaDied and specially adtpired was built of palest Parma violet-coloured silk, covered with tiny snowy ruchingsef white silk miaslin at intervals, Another, a pure white one was of satin, with iteur delis , in lace applied all over it, the tips of the ribs and the handle twine of cut crystal. Writing about it she says:
" It was in the summer
of 1888, not long after the death of my husband.
I had been used to keeping an oil lamp burning in my room for convenience during.the night. Ous night I alcidenially overturned the lamp, and a blaze kindled
man instant. Terrified half out of my wits I sprang from
bed, seized the burning articles and ran downstairs with them just in time to prevent further disaster. Happily for me I escaped with slight burns, but not from conse-
quonees of acother kind.
The fright and shock quite prostrated me. Do what
I would, after the danger was all over, I wa3 unable to
banish the subject from my thoughts. My nerves seemed completely unhinged, and I rapidly grew feeble, excitable, and debilitated. My appetite failed, and I
had 'no relish.for my ordinary food. There was a bad
taste in my mouth, headache, .distress after eating, loss of 119 sh and ambition, wi h a disposition to worry and
fret ovar things which, when I wAs well, had no 'luau-
en ee with nas whatever.
I sought to build up my
strength with beef tea and other notritiou3 and diges-
tible form 3 of diet, without success. "The doctors whom I consulted said I was suffering

from nervous debility and weakness. They gave me pre- scriptions, which the chemist made up for me; but they had no effect, and what I suffered I have no words to tell you. My health appeared to have been all broken

up suddenly, as a railway train goes to pieces in a col- lision. Month after mouth I struggled with this strange ailment, but could fled no remedy to relieve me. N4t until January, 1887, ,did I see my way out of the, trouble which followed my adventure of that fearful night. "At that time (January, 18871 I chanced to ceme upon a little book about Mother's Seigel's Syrup, as a cure for indigestion and dyspepsia. and the complaints attending it. Letters that were printed, in that book from others who had bcen cured by this remedy, gave me confidence, and I got a bottle from Mr. J. 11. Brown patent medicine dealer, 15, High-street, Margate. After taking it I felt decidedly better. I could eat and digest needed food my nerves were more under control, and I got better sleep and rest. I will merely add that, feeling sure that Mother Seigel's Syrup was helping me, I continued •te take it, and eventually recovered my health. For this I thank Mother Seigel's Syrup ; and if you think 83 singular an experience as mine would be of interest or use to any one, you may have my consent to publish it. (Signed) (Mrs.) C. L. Filmer, Thanet Cottage, Draper's Road, Margate, July 24h, 1895." Now I invite the reader's attention to a double fact; First (as is daily shown in these articles), that indiges- tion will disorder and disease the nervous system; and (second) that a violent shock to the nerous system will produce in lige4tion of a profound and intractable type. The latter fact is illustrated by the case we are now considering. There is no space here to treat of it at length. Let it suffice for the present that, either way, the remedy must be addressed to the digestion—not t the nerves. No competent physician treats a so-ealle I "nervous" disease as a nervous disease. He seeks for the location of the evil force, which is commonlys the stomach; corrects, that if he can, and leaves the nerves to right themselves as they always do. This is what Mother Seigel's Syrup did for Mrs. Filmer, and will do for you, in case (which Providence forbid) you are ever overthrown in like manner.

The general manager of the Glasgow tramways has reported to the Corporation of that city that the gross revonue in the year ending on the 31st ult. has been £334.378 13, 61. The working expenses have amounted to £250,827 174 9 i • leaving a balance of revenue over expenditure of £33,519 15a. 91. In the working expenses are ineluded the maintenance and renewal of perm inent way, buildings, horses. an 1 equipments. in addition to the ordinary expenses for hoesing, traffie, and general manalement. A considerable sum had been spent in Providing, temporary stable accommodation, and in altering and improving the depots to meet the require- ments of the augmented service. This expenditure the 'Committee have charged against revenue. -They have also charged against revenue the cost of canatruetin g additional sidings, crosa-overa 351.,and the whole of the 1 amount spent in the renewal of the permanent way. Ouitl of the balance of £83,519 15a. 91., the following suma have been nail to the common good :---interest on eapi- tal, £12,656 12s. 51. ; sinking fund. £10,541 19,. 2'. ; annual payment in lieu of rent, £9000: total. £32,198 73. This leaves a balance of £51,351 44. 21., and the Committee recommend that this sum be appropri- ated as follows :—Depreciation to be written off capi- tal. £17,941 15s. 61. ; permanent way renewal fend. £17.000 ; reserve fund for general purposes, £16,409 &. 81.; total, £51,351 44. 24. div.head: AMERICA.N PRESIDENCY.
div.p: THE AMERICA.N PRESIDENCY.

Mr. MeKinker, the candidate chosen by the Republican party for the United States Presidency, represents the (inlet type of American statesman. Until his name ha. came associated with high protection he was little known, although he had entered Congress in 1877. He wag a supporter of MoKinleyism long before that name was applied to the tariff Rill of 1890. which, as nhairman of the Ways and Means Committee, Mr. McKinley guided through Parliament. In Congress he proved a painstaking Member who was respected by both parties. He aspired to the Speakerahip, but was beaten by Mr. Reed, of Maine. It was the best thing which could have happened to him, as, according to custom, the Chairmanship of the Ways and Means Committee ' I'll to the defeated candidate, and with it came the oruntion of McKinleyiern, upon which Mr. McKinley's fame as a statesman rests. Like many other politicians which Ohir has produced, Mr. McKinley is of Scottish origin. His ancestors were Presbyterians,but he belong.; to the Methodist oiernpal Church. He was born in 1844—one of a gamily of nine. His school education was brief. When quite a boy he enttred the Army when the Civil War broke out. He won his military honours by his bravery, and was a major before he was twenty. After returning from the war he became a fairly successful lawyer in his native grate. His firat entry into public life was made in 1869 ; a year after he was coiled to the bar, when he was annninted to the modest office of county prosecut- ing attorney. He entered Congress as a reprrsentative of the Canton district of Ohio in 1877. He was defeated by the democratic triumphs which followed on MoKin- leyism, ht had the satisfaction of being elected Gover- nor of Ohio in the following year. Mr. McKinley has clear amt, striking features and has obtained the profix " Napoleon " owing to his" Napoleonic. "cage of man- tenance, and not on account of his ambition, or of his powers of generalship. He is the most striking persona- -1 litr who has arisen on the Republican side since Mr. Blaine. He hag not Blaine's magnetic influence, or his gift of oratory, hut has a capacity for taking pains, and 15 looked upon as a man of high character, who would nooke a thoroughly trustworthy, if not a brilliant President.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND' DISTRICT FOOT-
div.p: WARRINGTON AND' DISTRICT FOOT-
BALL ASSOCIAnoN.
ANNUAL MEETING.

At the Roebuck H )tel, Warrington, on Tuesday eyen- leg, the annual general meeting in connew-ion with the Warrington and District Football Association was held. The bUsi new; of the meeting consisted in the considera- tion of the rules of the Association, the electinn of offi- cers and executive for the ensuing season. There was a good attendance of representatives of utubs in War- rington and district. Mr. WHITTLE, of Barnton, was voted to the chair. SECRETARY'S REPORT. _ _ .

The Seceemne-read his annual report in which he stated that he was happy to say that he could with con- fidence congratulate the Association on the prey,ress made so far as football was concerned. Re was, how- ever, sorry to say that the finances had suffered con- siderably, as the treasurer's report showed, and the executive were endeavouring to meet this contingency by proposing slight alterations in the rules of the Associ- ation and also of the Cup competition. - During the past year the Association had had a ineethership of 41 clubs, of which 27 entered for the " Observer r' competition,thel remaining 14 clubs being affiliated only. This compared f avourably with the previous year, when the Associa- tion included a membership of 29 club e all of • which • competed for the Cup. The Exe- cutive proposed a scheme during the football year to form a Junior Medal Competition, but it fell through owing to the delay in getting the necessary permission- from the senior asspciation, which at first gave only a half-hearted permission, curtailing the radius of the competition to six miles. The Executive promptly appealed against this and, when the competition was opened to the full extent of the association's radius of, ten Miles, the proposition • fell through. The funds of the association had also a distinct bearing on the project and he had no doubt the Esecutive would heartily co-operate with the clubs in promoting the scheme for ' the benefit of the junior clubs • and reserve teams. Several cases of misconduct of players on the fi.dcl of play had been dealt with by the Executive and in some Cases the referee had been threatened and met With hostile treatment at the hands of the players, who, no doubt, had been incited to such acts of violence by over- heated spectators. The Executive had emphasized their intention to deal strongly with these cases. Any further cases that might come before them would be justly but severely dealt with as such scenes were becoming com- mon and were a disgrace to sport and football alike. The Executive had during the year found it necessary to elect Mr. T. P. Brnadhurst to fill the vacancy for the Warrington General Division caused by the resignation of Mr. W. T Porter who had unfortunately lost the use of his eyesight. The Executive conveyed their sym- pathy with the affeted gentlemen and no doubt the clubs, and thme who knew Mr. Porer would be sorry to hear of his affi ction.—The report was unanimously adopted. . •

In this stare if. a man steals a loaf, he would very likely have to live on prison fare and wear motley but if he murders a girl, or. as there have been quite a number of cases recently, he ravishes mere children, why it will be no'one's business to make him suffer, and he may indefinitely, live on the fat of the land.

• Liberty, yes, 'tie a sweet land of liberty. In poli- tics the honest politician is a crank, and looked, upon as a foot, because he neither helps himself nor anyone else to the loaves and fishes. America will never know what liberty is until the press is made to know what slander is. True liberty will never belong to the American people until newspaper enterprises in the shape of interviewing' is brought into reasonable bounds. Cases occur every day where people object to being interviewed. All the same copy is found to cover a column. -In my opinion in nine cases out of ten the newspapers try the criminal, and I am quite sure, in the same pro- portion, they. thwart justice. Let the press once get alter a man, or woman, or Corporation, and, it matters not right or wrong, it never loses sight until ruin is in view. This is liberty as Americans see it. During the years I have lived in California a number of societies have been formed for the pur- pose of insisting on the law being carried oat:They all come to nought. As a rule the native son cares only to go into that that has dollars in it. He is never patriot enough to sacrifice his nurse for his country's good.He will bellow like a mad hull,when the" blarsted Britisher" insists upon liberty for all at the Cape,or if he thinks there is a chance to gain a few of the almighty dollars. For these be would sell his soul, and daily he sells his country. To-day America is in the hands of aliens, or to a large pro- portion it is In the hands of those whose fathers came from over the sea, and whose chief interest is to make the country the home of a religion that never knew what liberty was in any sense of the word. 11. BY ME. ki. WHITHAM. At a public meeting recently held hero' one of the speakers brought the house down, when he pro- ceeded to tell how his Parents, years ago. left Eng- land, a land where State church, and Royalty leagued with a bloated aristocracy to grind the people underfoot. And when he proceeded to tell his wildly enthusiastic audience that they were citizens of the only country Mt earth that knew What political freedom was, be sure he was very near receiving a nomination for any post his admir- ing listeners had to give away. When I raid these vapourings, that are thrown broadcast among the people by editor and politician, I smile a pretty broad smile and remember Barnum's statement, " The American people .like to be humbugged." But what becomes of the ceputation the native son is supposed to have gain-qi for cuteness? Well, like a good many other reputations it has its shady side and thereby hangs many a tale, and they are not all of the , wooden nutmeg sort. Once upon a time, as the story teller puts it, I could shout with the loudest," Down with the Queen, down with the state, clown with the church, down with every- thing-that's up,and up with,everything that's down.' Now. I should modify this a little, and, just looking round to see who was listening. I should whisper rather hesitatingly, " D awn with the church "but "God bless. the Queen and may she live for ever." What a confession to make after near ten years residence in the "Greatest Republic on earth." Pos- sibly there are lots more who could make just such a statement, only "they don't like." Well whether like it or not,! feel I must do it, because, writing with thikohject of at least trying to ins•ruct, I see thatonly that way truth lies. But nnw, the reason for all this change in opin- ion. The reasOns are manifold, and not to be given by rote. Or, in giving them we may be thought to qualify some of the above. Do I prefer mon- arch to a president? That depends very much upon the sort of monarch we have in view, and his powers. There are one or two in Europe whose power seem to be abolished, and of whom a large majority of Europeans Would say, could they have the chance, "the world could get on very well with- out them" But, when a monarch of the British lion type, with claws clipt and a growl that has to he brought up right from the gutter to the purple before it dare he uttered is in question, why then I say I don't see much diff oN.ne.e, or, if any, it is in favour of the British throne as against the Ameri- can presidential chair. div.head: SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO CAPTAIN BUCKTON.
div.p: SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO CAPTAIN BUCKTON.

Captain Bnckton, solicitor, of the firm of Messrs. Greenall and Buckton, Win wick-t., Warrington, met with a serious accident on Thursday evening by falling from his horse.lt appears that he was pro- ceeding over Bank Quay bridge on horseback about 7.30 p.m. with the object of travelling to Pentteth for the purpose of inspecting a church lads' brigade, when he lost possession of his hat. Whether in endeavouring to recover it he fell from his horse, or whether he was thrown from the animal's back is net known, buts he alighted heavily on the macadamised road with his head, and his face was badly injured. Sergeant Rowbottom and Police Constables Barnett and Leonard were within easy distance fled rendered prompt assist- ance. Fortunately, Mr. Sadler, son of the Mayor of Widnes, was passing in a trap at the time, and he at.once jumped out and offered his vehicle to con- vey the injured gentleman to the Infirmary. Sergeant Rowbottom assisted Captain Buckton into the trap, and on arrival at the Infirmary, Dr.tang- eiale, the senior house surgeon, immediatly ex- amined the injuries and found that Captain Buck- ton was suff-:ring from concussion of the brain.
