div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
FAILURE OF A RUNCORN TRADESMAN.

Joseph Tickle residing at 5, Alcock-street. Runcorn, lately residing and carrying on business at 17, Bridge- street, as hardware dealer and confectioner, filed his petition of bankruntcy at Warrington on Tuesday.
THH ROYAL SHOW AT LHICHSTER.-SUCCESSFUL LOCAL
EXHIBIT

In the class for colts !cote(' in 1896 at the above slow Mr. S. B. Chadwick, of Runcorn, took first prize with his chessnut foal, Hawthorn Dale, Lord Egerton of Tatton's colt being third in the same class. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The annual sermons on behalt of the above church were preached on Sunday in the above church. The morning preacher was the Vicar (the Rev. Dr. Preston) while the evening sermon was preached by the R,-v. H. C. Moyle, M.A., of the Parish Church clergy staff. ST. JOHm'S BAPTIST SCHOOL, WESTON.

As advert'sed, special services will be held in the St. Edward's Catholic Church, Runcorn, on Sunday next on behalf of St. John's Baptist School, Weston. Two ser- mons will be preached by the Rev. Father Day, S J., who is the son of Mr. Justice Day, the celebrated judge.
PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.

At a reeent meeting held in Shaw-street School, a handsome pencil case was presented to Mrs Poole, who is about to leave Runcorn. The gift had been sub- scribed by the members of the mothers' meeting over which Mrs. Poole had presided in the absence of Mrs. Wood whom she had previously assisted.
SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN CYCLIST.

On Wednesday, C. Johnson, of Runcorn, secured the first prize in the two miles bicycle handicap at the Lytham sports. Mr. Johnson was alsa succeesful on Saturday in gaining a gold medal, representing the second prize for the two miles bicycle handicap in the sports under the auspices of the Hadfield Cricket and Lawn Tennis Club.

ST. LUKE'S CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN. On Sunday the anniversary serviced in connection with the above school were held. Both at the morning and evening services the Rev. E. Austin, of Widnes, preached to good clngregaticns in the Bethesda Church, and in the afternoon the preacher delivered an interest- ing address to teachers, scholars and parents. The col- lections throughout the day realised about £7, which will be devoted to the sc'dool funds. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. RUNCORN.

On Sunday special flower services wilihe held in the Bethesda Church, Runcorn. Two sermons will be preached by the Rev. J. Simpson, whose subject in the evening will be" A Summer Sermon." At the evening service in addition to the usual musical programme there will be a solo by Mrs. Temperley. Gifts of flowers for the services will be welcomed. Full particulars will be found in our advertising columns.

THE PROPOSED ROAD TO WESTON POINT.

At a meeting of the Highway Committee of the Run- corn Urban District Council on. Wednesday, it was re- ported that a communication had been received from Major Orred's agent to the effect that he could not com- ply with the wishes of the Council with rezard to the land for the proposed vehicular road to Weston Point from Runcorn. It was decided to appoint a committee to ascertain whether the four-foot road to be provided by the Canal Company could not be made to the width of 24ft.

div.head: RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN CYCLING CLUB.

The members of the Runcorn Cycl.ng Club turnld out on Saturday tor Bedford Leigh whicli place vras duly reached. The journey ti the destination and the attrac- tions of ths place were thoroughly enj wed, the return journey being made in good time. The Wednesday sec tion elected to go to Beeitnn, Wednesday being a festival day, and the ten memb-rs who started were amply repaid the trouble of the journey by the attractions afforded on the gala ground. CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR SOCIETY PICNIC AT RUNCORN. The annual outing in connection with the Society of Christian Endeavour belonging to the t llesmere United Methodist Free Church, Runcorn, took place on Satur- day afternoon. Rock Savage was the destination of a large party, the yQunget members of which were taken in a lurry kindly lent by Mr. Stubbs. A field was placed at the disposal of the party by Mr. Joseph Stokes, and a pleasant afternoon w4s spent in outdoor recreation. During the afternoon refreshments were provided.

div.head: BEGGING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: BEGGING AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court before Messrs. J. Hand- ley and F. J. Norman, on Wednesday morning, William Brown, a tramp, was charged with begging in Church- et., at one o'clock on Tuesday.—P.C. Gregory stated the circumstances.—Prisoner pleaded not guilty and main- tained that he was not begging and could bring proof of his statement. In order to allow prisoner to call wit- nesses a remand was granted until Thursday morning.— On Thursday morning prisoner was again charged before Mr. James Handley and failing to bring his witnesses was sent to goal for 12 days hard labour.

div.head: FRFQUENTING "AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FRFQUENTING "AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday morning before Messrs. J. Handley and F. J. Norman, at the Runcorn Police Court, John T. Cross,a stranger to the town was charged with frEquent- ice the neighbourhood of Thomas-st.,the night previous with intent to commit a felony.—P.C. Gregory said that he was on duty at Delph Bridge. Runcorn, on Tuesday evening and saw prisoner standing about the backs of the houses in Irwell-lan He watched the prisoner and saw him go down an entry between Stanley and Parker- at., and try the back doors. He afterward.; went to the back door of the Wilson Hotel, and went into the yard. Prisoner an coming out noticed that he was being watched, hurried, but (he witness) arrested him and talk him to the police sta.tion.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for one months' bard labour.
INTERESTING WEDDING AT RI7NCORR.

On Wednesday afternoon at the Runcorn Parish Church the Rev. H. B. Firth jn,ned together Sarah E Bebbington, eldest dauThter of Mr. John Behhingten, of Runcorn, and Samuel Miller,son of Mr.J.Miher, of Top ockg, Runcorn. The bride,who was given away by her father, was attired in a shot alpaca dress, trim- med with silk and white hat trimmed with white tip;. She also carried a bouquet of biennia. the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids—Miss S. Miller, sister of the bride and Miss A. Wilson—were attired in fawn coloured dresses, trimmed with shot silk, and white bats with white tips. After the ceremony the happy couple were warmly congratulated by many of their assembled friends, and the party afterwards adjourned to the house of the bride's father where luncheon was provided. The newly married couple left Runcorn for Irackpool, en route for the Isle of Man the same after- noon. - -

- • RESCUE FR3li DROWNIFIG AT RUNCORN. On Thursday at noon, a child aged three years, a son of Henry Moores, one of the constables of the Bridge- water Trustee, at Top Locks, narrowly escaped drown- ing. The child was playing on the canal side at Top Lock when he fell in and his position became extrernely perilous. As the child was sinking for the second time, Mr. George Pickstock, of Wellington-st., had come upon the scene. He jumped into the water and shortly suc- ceeded in bringing the child to the side. Great praise is due to Mr. Pickstock for the heroism he displayed and particularly as considering that on Wednesday he re- famed work after suffering from sciatica for six weeks. Mr. Pickstock has already been instrumental in saving the lives of a woman and child at Rochdale, and three men at Liverpool.

SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN. On Thursday afternoon gr. W. Warsley held an in- quest at the Runcorn PONCA Station, on Elizabeth Joyn- son, aged 55, who died suddenly at 19, Princess-it .on Tuesday morning.—Joseph Joynson living at 19, Prin. cess-st., Runcorn, labourer, said that deceased was his wife aged 55 years. She had been ailing for the last 20 ysars, hut she had not been seen by a docter for some- thing like 12 months. . She had been troubled with heart disease and 12 months ago she had A stroke. Before her death there had been no symptoms. His daughter found her dead, sitting in an outhouse on the 23rd June. —Bertha Joynson a daughter of the deceased, said about nine o'clock on Tuesday morning she went out in her usual state of health, and shq went to look for her ten minutee afterwards and found her dead, sitting on the seat.—Dr. McLeneon, said he had known deceased for several years, and had attended her several timcs. She was suffering from a disease of the heart. He believed the cause of death was suddeu failure of the heart's action. A verdict according to! the medical .testimony was returned.

div.p: FINANCIAL AND MINING NOTES.

" We understand that the Manager of the Rand Reefs Company is now on a hurried visit to this country in order to consult the directors on the position of the company as affected by recent important developments. It is stated that the manager is engaged upon a report of the present position of the property, which w;11 be issued to the shareholders in a short time, and is likely to be of a very satisfactory character. It may be that we have here an explanation both of the recent buying and the ready absoiption of Rand Reefs, and, under the circumstances, it would be as well for the Directors to publish the report without delay. " Financial News" June 25th.

TYPHUS FEVER AT HALTON.

Mr. Farrington reported that he had written to Dr. Hope; medical officer of Liverpool, stating,—that he was directed by the Medical Officer of Health to inform him that they had had six cases of typhus fever, in their district, the whole of which bad been in a family, which had recently been residing in Hyslop-street.off Toxteth-road Liverpool, and asking him to inform them if such a fever had been prevalent in the localit named and also if the schools in the neighbourhood had been closed, owing to an epidemic of some kind. He received a reply dated June 18, from Dr. Hope, who said that tpphus fever had occurred in the locality named for several months past and that it owed its dissemination in all probability to one of the schools in the district. The measures taken for the suppression of the disease were successful but each week a few cases had been dis- covered and removed to hospital. The number under treatment in hospital at the present time was 29.—Dr. Adams medical officer said that they had seen the last of the outbreak. It had very probably not arisen from any insanitary condition of the premises but had been ins ported from Liverpool

div.head: RITNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COIJCIL.
div.p: RITNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COIJCIL.

A special meeting of this Council was held on Monday morning in the Town Hall. There were present :—Mr. J. W.Lightburn, J.P. (in the chair), Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C Ald. H. J. Grice, W. Handley, J. Horsefif Id, W. Bisbrown, W. Collier, J. Pritchard, F. Wiswall, G. Hewitt,J. Wilson, Rev. Dr. Gestelib, E. Marshall (secre- tary), P. A. Like (law clerk), J. Wilding (surveyor). The object of the meeting was to pass such rasolutions as might be deemed advisable in respect of the Manches- ter Ship Canal Bill and the Local Government Provi- sional Order (Ports) Bill. The Council at once decided to go into committee,and an hour elapsed before the meeting was, made public to the reporters. The Chairman said it would be in the recollection of the Council that Mr. Lake and himself were autherised to go to London in support of the petition against the Bill promoted by the Local Government Board for the formation of a Port Sanitary Authority for Manchester in which Runcorn was included. Mr. Speakman had heard in Manchester that there was to be a conference between the Manchester Corporation and the Local Government Board, and he urged Mr. Lake and himself to go to London and endeavour to influence the result of the deliberations. They went to London on Wednes- day evening and met Mr. Speakman at ten o'clock. They proceeded to their Parliamentary agents and also saw the agent for the Rural Coencil an gave instructions indicating that they meant to fight vigor- ously against the Bill, and that they were determined to fightwith real shot and not charge their weapons with buttermilk. (Laughter.) That no doubt had its effect upon the result of the delihelations of the conference. The deputation saw Mr. Southern, who represented the. Manchester Corporation and also the Ship Canal Com- pany, and they received an intimation that the portion of the Bill including Runcorn in the Port Sanitary Auth- ority had been dropped. This meant that for the next four or five years Runcorn would be entirely excluded from any payments to the authority and there was a promise given that when the order was amended the other riparian authorities such as Elhennere Port,Widnes ' and Warrington would be brought it to pay their quota of the expense of the maintenance and the establish- ment of the Port Sanitary Authority. He (the chair- man) attached particular importance to that because the object of the Council was to strenuously oppose the con- tribution of one twentieth of the expense on Runcorn, while other authorities which would receive equal bene- fits would not pay one penny to the cost. in their peti- tion the Council urged that the other authorities should be brought in and pay their fair share, which was a most equitable prayer. On any future order the Manchester people would take care that these riparian authorities were included. He ought not to neglect to inform them and to express a strong feeling of the appreciation of the kindness the deputation received at the hands of Mr. Southern and the great interest he exhibited to re- move from Runcorn all charges which might possibly be done. Mr. Southern's action with respect to Runcorn was of the most friendly character, for which they ought to be very much obliged, He was sure Mr. Southern's desire to do all he could for Runcorn tended very much to the favourable conditions in which they found themselves that morning. (Applause.) Mr. Grice moved that the Cluncil do approve of the action in London of the dPputation appointed to take all necessary steps in support of else Council's petition against the Local Government's Provisional Order (Ports) Bill, before the House of Commons Committee. Mr. Grice expressed satisfaction that they had been treated in such a fair and just manner by the Manches- ter Corporation, and he had no doubt that in future they would receive every consideration from the Manchester people. The town had a good many interests invested with the Manchester Ship Canal, in fact all the interests of the town were identical with those of the canal, and it would be wise for the Council to promote the success of that undertaking and in so doing they would add to the town's benefit.
Mr Collier seconded the resolution, and thought that the thanks of the ratepayers and the Council were due to the chairman and the law clerk for the action they had taken in this matter.
The Chairman : I would like to include Mr. Speakman in the motion.

Mr. Collier said he would include Mr. Speakman in it if that gentleman particularly desired it. He pointed out that they had acted contrary to the advice or Sir John Brunner who had recommended the Council to drop the opp)sition ; in fact, the Chairman took a strong lead in the matter and had it not been for his single-minded action, backed up by the law clerk, he was certain Run- corn would not have saved the large amount of money annually which they wont I now save. When there was a chance of showing the ratepayers how the committee and officials worked for the interest of the town it ought to be taken advantage of in every possible form.
Mr. Pritchard supported the resolution and remarked that from £.115 to £l2O a year would be saved by the action of the committee.

Mr. Bisbrown also supported the motion remarking that Sir J. Brunner told them there was no chance of successfully opposing the Local Gavernment Board, but the matter had been opposed, and they had staved off the payment of a heavy sum, for,five or six years. He endorsed all that had been said about the friendly feel- ing that had existed between the Council and the Ship Canal Company. During the negotiation With reference to the graving dock, and the slipways, the Manchester people seemed anxious to come to a compromise and sPttle the matter in an amicable manner,and give reason- able terms. The friendly feeling ought to be recip- roeated by the Council.

Dr. Gastaldi in suppnrting the resolution said great praise was due to the Committee that had taken this matter in hand. lilt had not been for six or seven members who were detormined to carry on the opposi- tion to the order, th 9 thibg would have collapsed all to- gether. While the Council rej Aced with the deputation's success they ought not to forget the men who had worked for it. Re himself proposed that the Council fight the erfle.., and he was pleased on behalf of the rate- payers that the opposition had been successful.

Mr. Collier : I quite forgot you, Doctor. (Laugh- ter). Mr. Handley said as Sir J. Brunner and the advice he I gave had been referred to he would point out that the very thing Sir J. Brunner had predicted had come to Pass. Sir John advised them that if they withdrew their oppesition and not cause the order to be made into :in Act of Parliament, that the order would come up in an amended form at some future time. After Sir John gay') his advice the whole circumstances were entirely changed by the Rural Authority determining to go on with their ovositinn,and Sir John was informed of that and from that time had been doing his utmost to carry out what the Council wished a few days ago. He did not want a vote of thanks. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Handley) wrote to Sir John ry?inting out that the Run- corn Urban Council were prepared to deal with all port sanitary cases at their own hespital.and was successfully treating one at the present time, and it was conse- quently rather hard that they should be called upon to Par any proportion of the cost of the Manchester order. The reply he received from Sir John proved to him (Mr. Handley) that he had represented this fact to the pro- per quarter,and had recommended such a course as had now been followed. He had great pleasure in giving his meed of °raise to the chairman, Mr. Speakman, and the law elerk in having acted so promptly in this matter, and he hoped that when the order came up in an amPnded form it would be so just and equitable that no upnnsitinn.would be needed.

The Chairman said they must give come owed of praise to the Rural Council for what they had done. Alludine to Sir John Brunner, he said if they had ac- cepted his advice the order would have been left as it stood and Runcorn would have had to contribute a share of the cost. When they found that the Rural Council were determined to oppose the order and force it into Parliament the Urban Council petitioned also and the Local Government Board asked the Manchester nenple if they would support the order by eyidenc.,with a result that a conference was held and the disputed clauses withdrawn.

Mr. Grine said at the time Sir John gave his advice it waq understood that they would have to fight the Local Government Board which was :4 strong rower to fight hot it appeared they had had to fight the Manches- ter peonl P.

Mr. Sp,akman said he had opportunity of brineing the matter before the chairman and Mr. Lake and he took advantage of it, and as he was in London on county hnsiness he impressed upon thoae gentlemen the necessity of acting upon the information he imparted, and he congratulated the Council upon the success they had obtained. This resolution was then carried unanimously and the meeting concluded.

div.head: FUNERALS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FUNERALS AT RUNCORN.

The remains of the late Mr. Robert Shingler, aged 54, of Albert-st., were interred in the cemetery, Runcorn, on Tuesday afternoon. The deceased was well known as caretaker of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Greenway- road, where he had served in that capacity since the church was built. The funeral service was partly con- ducted in thQ nouse of the deceased, the concluding part of the service being read at the graveside. The Rev. T. Bramell officiated. The bearers were Messrs. Jabez Stubbs, Robert Stubbs, A. Shingler, G. Sbingler, J.Shing- ler, F. Shingler, R. Owen. There were also present at the funeral Mr. G. Shingler, and W. S. Shingler (brothers), Mr. W. The body of Mr. Joseph Hayes, late Cross-street, Run- corn, was laid to rest in the Runcorn Cemetery on Wednesday, the Rev. T. Bramall being the officiating clergyman. Mr. Hayes was also a member of the Primi- tive Methodist Church,Greenway-road, and was well re- spected by the members of the congregation.

The funeral of the late Mr. Thomas Marshall took place at the Runcarn Cemetery on Tuesday afternoon. The deceased died on Saturday at the age of 61 years at his residence in Brackley-street. He was employed on the Bridgewater Canal undertaking and had served that canal company for over 20 years. The funeral ceremony was attended by Messrs. R. Rawlinson and Powell representing the employees of the Canal Company and there was a large gathering of relatives and friends and a number of members of St. Paul's Church, with which the deceased was prominently identified. The Rev. W. George conducted the services.

div.head: CONiPLATETS FROM THE ASYLUM
div.p: CONiPLATETS FROM THE ASYLUM

Mr. A. Hornby, Clerk to the Committee of the County Asylum had forwarded a circular letter calling attention to the fact that sevaral instances had occurred of late in which patients had been sent to the asylum suffering only from senile dementia attributable to old age and ap- parently sent only to die—in fact, death had occurred within a very few days after admission accelerated in many instances by such removals. Mr. Hornby asked that in future cases, the greatest possible care should be taken in the selection of patients to be sent to the asylum. In the second communication Mr. Hornhy pointed out that the asylum was practically full, and he requested that, before sending patients,relieving officers should ascertain by telegram whether there was accom- modation.
It was decided to send copy of the letter to the re- lieving officers.

Jacks-is preached a suitable sermon, the lessons being read by Captain McKecknie and Lieutenant- Surgeon Murray. The lads, after the service, were m imbed back to the village and there dismissed. OVER.—On Saturday the members of the Warrington Liberal Club bowling team paid a visit to Over, near Winsford, in return for the visit of the Over team to Warringten a fortnight ago. Some of the membirs went by rail and some by road, the sixteen-mile drive through Delamere being greatly enjoyed by the latter party. div.head: SHIP CANAL
div.p: SHIP CANAL
LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC.

During the week ended June 19 the number of sea- going cargo vessels arriving at and sailing from the port. of Manchester was 172, representing an aggregate net registered tonnage of 40.244 tons. In the preceding week the figures were 193 ships, 47,664 tons. One hun- dred and forty-one ships of 22,412 tons were Pngaged in the coastwi e trade, as against 159 ships of 27,376 tone in the previous week, whilst 31 ships of 17,832 tons were in trade with foreign ports, as againel. 34 ships or 20.488 tons. The principal arrivals from foreign ports- included wheat from the River Plate, bone-ash from Rio Grande do Sul, timber from Campbeltown, N. 8., and Riga, woodpulp from Skein and Christiania, logwood, from Laguna, flints front Cherbourg, St. Valery, an& Treport, and general cargo from Rotterdam, Boulogo6, Rouen, Paris, Antwerp, Hamburg, and New York. TWO steamers sailed with general cargo for the Brazils, a barque cleared for Shediac, N. 8., and steamers left the canal for Treport, Hamburg, Stettin Copenhagen, Rot- terdam, Ghent, Helsingfors, Christiania, and Boulogne. THE ASSESSMENT OF THE BRIDGEWATER CANAL.

At a meeting of the Assessment Committee of the Runcorn Union held at Dutton on Tuesday, under the chairmanship of Mr.H.E. Heywood,the Manchester Ship Canal Company appealed against tne assess:.le.nt of the Bridgewater Canal. The length of the canal inthe Union is from beyond Warrington to Weston Point. Mr. W. H. Collier, the general manager appeared on behalf of the Company and placed figures before the committee show— ing a reduction in receipts which he thought warranted a reducti'm in the assessment. Alter some considera- tion the sulject was adjourned in order that the Council might act in concert with the other unions through whose districts the waterway passed. REPORT OF THE MANCHESTER CORPORATION ENGINEER.

The Special Committee of the Manchester Corporation will present a report to the City Council on Wednesday next, in which is embodied the following report from Mt. G. H. Hill, the engineer for the Corporation. It is for the quarter ending 31st March, 1896 I only pre- pose in this report to give a short summary of capital expenditure on works and equipment for the three moinths, and to bilvfly mention the progress which has been made since Jinuary in the development of the undertaking. I think it better to leave anything like a detailed statement to be dealt with in the report to be submitted after the next hall-yearly alance-sheet of the Canal Company is isgued.

CAPITAL EXPENDITURE ON NEW WORKS AND EQUIPMENT. —The dpproxim ,te amount expended during the three months has been small, being about £15,000, the main items being for a new tug for the traffic department and payments on account of new electric light installation,,. new hydrtulic instsllation, Bunsen] las-bves, and new dock for Ellesmere Port pontoon, the rest being for sun- dry small matters of equipment. WORKING EXPENSES —The expenditure under revenue- accr.unt is within the amount estimated as necessary. Mow WORKS.— I he new warehouses being erected by the Manchester Ship Canal Warehousing Company are- nearing completion, and are Partially in use, hut I donor, expect they will be finally finished before July. They will prrwe a great benefit to the shed capacity. DREDGINO.—The ameunt expended on maintenance dredging up to the 31st March was about £10.&00; this- is under the amount estimated, but it is too early to say if this well be the due proportion for the whole year. LATCHFORD Loot GATES.—The lock gates carried away by tte: Harold have ',evil repaired, and the new ones (to- be temporarily used while the upper gates are taken out of the canal to be overhauled) are nearly complete. Both pair,' will be shortly placed in position. BRIDGES &c.—The bridges are being repainted in tern, and all structures on the canal and Liucks are efficienTly maintained.

TYAFFIC.—The traffic centinues to expand in an en- couragitie manner, the t,.tsl tonnage dealt with from Jdnna:v 1 to Maret 31, 1896,being 394.492 to , s,against 280.756 tons in 1895 the receipts for the first three montbs were £36 984 in 1896, against £27,216 in 1895. Me increase being about 40 pr cent. on tonnage and 3'3 per eent. on revenue. A disappointing feature in the traffic is the inaction at rartinßtnn Coal Basin. COM- paratively little is toing done there,nctwithstanding the fdct that it is the nearest port to the Lancashire coal- fields, and considerable c Ipital was expended there to meet the prebelle Ti quirem,,nts. AFRICAN WARS :-A PROTEST.

We the Society of Friends in Lancashire and Cheshire, assembled in our district meeting, feel it to be our duty to express ouremphatic condemnation of the wars which have been, and are now being waged in the name of our country on the African Continent. We hold these wars to be unrighteous and un-Christian. We maintain that the destruction of comparatively unarmed people by modern machines of warfare is both ignoble and cruel. We are convinced that unbrotherly treatment of native races cannot be justified on the plea of territorial expan- sion for ourselves, or of possible civilization for these races. Believing that the principles taught by Jesus Christ are the principles on whi ,h all true progress must be based, we earnestly appeal to our fellow-Christians to join us in protesting against a policy in which these principles are openly ignored. Signed in, and on behalf of, the aforesaid meting, held at Lancaster, the 17th and 18th of sixth month, JOHN P. LEATHER, clerk.

div.head: STATE OF SANKEY BROOK.
div.p: THE STATE OF SANKEY BROOK.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me a small space in your Saturday's issue to call attention to the state of Sankey Brook atSankey Bridges. It is a matter of great import- anee that steps should be taken forthwitn by the re- sponsible parties in authority for the comfort and health of this neighbourhood to put a stop for ever to the dis- gracefnl state of this brook. The question which is so often brought up and discussed, only to fall again with- out an attempt to relieve the long felt wants of the people living almost on the banks of this filthy smelling stream,ef black, sometimes blue, sometimes yellow filth, I is one that should not be allowed to exist for one week much less to be a perpetual nuisance to everyb-xly in close proximity and all who have occasion to pass through Sankey Bridges where people coming up from town by no means walk or ride leisurely past. Many are the loud complaints and expressions of wonder that people can live near and endure itor sit still and make no effort to rid themselves of the pest. Whatever the causes— whether they be owing to the alkali refuse being washed down from St. Helens—l am not in a position to say.but that is the prevailing idea. If it be so, I say some representations should be made to the manufac- turers to stop this nuisance. It is cruel that innocent people should be made to suffer for their benefit. What- ever means are adopted to dispense with the refuse, it should at any rate not be to the disadvantage of the people living far from its origin.—Yours truly, HEALTH. June 25th, 1896.
ATTEMPTED SUICIDES AT WAR RINGTO N.

Before Mr. R. Garnett at the Warrington Borough Court,on Tuesday, John Bolan, aged 56, Back Dallam- lane, was chargcd with attempting to commit suicide on Monday by taking poison. The Chief Constable said the whole affair seemed to 'nave been more or less a result of temper. He did not purpose to go into any evidence at all. About 220 on Monday afternoon defendant's wife was getting his dien( r ready when he came in and said, "I shan't want any dinner; I shan't be here in twenty minutes." He then went into the back yard. A lodger named Michael Bolan went in the same direction and saw defendant fall. Defendant's wife went to him, but he made an obscene remark and she went for assistance. A young woman named Theresa l!llrris went to him an-I ho said he had taken rat poison. Dr. Adams was sent for, and gave defendant an emetic. Defendant was sent to the Infirmary where he had been under the care of Dr. Langdale, and in the custody of the police. Ser- geant Rowbottom asked him what he had done it for -and he said, "I have done it for vexation." He ap- peared very sorry. It was said that for some time back he had been giving way t, drink and intemperate habits that did not conform with his you s. Defendant, who looked at least ten years oiler than he said, and was still suffering from the effects of drink and the poison, said " I !am very sorry for it an,i do not know what made me do i. The Chief Constable : They In it to frightea their wives, and their wives to frighten their husbands. When suioidLifsucceed.i they do not make such a parade of preliminaries. Mrs. Bolan said defendant had been taking drink since Christmas. If he kept from dri!,k thore was not a better man anywhere. He worked at Nlesrs. Evans coal-yard. A young man had lately rog,ued nit of some money and he had been despondent. He was in drink on Mon- day when he did this foolish act. Defendant ; " I could not help it at the time." Mr. Garnett : You know " when the drink's in wit'S out." The Chief Constable : I think he hurt himself more than he intended. I ask tor a week's remand in cus- tody. I, ill get the drink out .DF him. D'efend ant : lamin a poor sate if I stop here. The Chief Constable : You a% ill be taken to Strange- -wars where you will he takii r 02 of. Mr. G3rnett then remanded B )lan as requested.

On Thursday morning at the Warrinxton Police Court 'before the Mayor, Alderman Sutton, Colonel Ridgway, and Mr. S. Chandley, a young man named Charles Hot- den, 72 Longford-st. wai charged with attompting to •om mit suicide by cutting his throat on the 18th inst. The Chief Constable. said the defendant stood charged with attrwopting to commit suicide by cutting his throat .and also with taking poison. From enquiriol which!had beim made he came to the conclusion that at the time the attempt was made defendant was non compog meiztis and he simply brought the matter before the benell for .the fact to be stated. Defendant's father was a widower and be lived with him. On Thursday morning between one and two o'clock they should have occupied the same bed. The father woke up and missed the defend int. He heard him making a peculiar noise dewnwtairs and went after him. He found defendant on the sofa and 'bleeding from a slight incised wound on the left of his throat. He said to the defendant " What liaNq you done this for " and the latter pointed to a letter on the ,table. This had since been destroyed but he (the Chief Constable) understood it to have said" Deaf father for- give me for the rash act I have done, give my love to all." The tattier saw that the defendant was suff,,ring more than wa.et attributable to the ctr, and lo .kifer round saw a bottle on the table containin..; spirits of Baits. Be at once gave defendant some whiteninu and water, and sent for Dr. Adams who managed to bring - defandin; round. 110 now expressed very deep s••rrow for the act he had committed. He had been low in his mind and had had pains in his head. The night prt.yin„, cricket and seemed in the 1-pst f he had been playing health. Impuliie was apparently the explanatich. Defendant's father said he did not think tie wouut ever do anything of the sort again he had suffered so much during the week. lie had never shown any enema' weakness before but through , being out of work some 12 months he had been depressed. The Chief Constable said Dr. Adams had told him that he did not think defendant .had any intention to take his life but had done the at hysterically with the in- tention of exciting sympathy. The magistrates dismissed the defendant with a cau- ,tion.

div.head: POLICE CASES
div.p: POLICE CASES

At the Earlestown Police ,Station on Monday morning before Mr. J. W. Emmett, David McMaster of Newton, was charged with being drunk and in- capable in Suez-street, at 12.30 p.m. on Saturday. He had to be conveyed to the police station in a hand cart, and was fined 24. 61. and costs. Luke Dowell at the same court was charged with beg- ging in Sankey-street on Sunday, and was com- mitted for 7 days.

CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR PICNIC, The Newton Congregational branch of the Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour had a pic- nic on Saturday to Lymrn. The party, numbering about 30, left Newton about two o'clock in a couple of wagonettes and on arrival at Lymm, had tea at a farm house. After a pleasant ramble about Lymm, they started for home at 8.30, having thoroughly enjoyed the outing.
NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING.-A PLUCKY
RECITE.

On Friday evening a little boy, two years of age. named Ferguson, living in Wargrave-road, when playing by the side'of wnat is known as Thompson's pit accidently fell in. A young lady named Miss Gertrude Price who was passing at the time, seetng the child struggling in the water, pluckily entered the pit, and at a great ri,k to herself, rescued the child and brought it to the bank, where two boys named Williams and Sankey assisted her out. The child was not much the worse for its immersion. TRADESDIEN'S PICNIC FROM EARLESTOWN. The second annual picnic of the tradesmen of Earlestown took place ou Thursday under very favourable circumstances. Something like 60 left Earlestown by the 8.45 train in two spacious saloons for Lancaster. On arrival there the party visited and inspected the Castle, afterwards setting out in waggonettes for Morecambe. An excellent dinner was served at the Clarendon Hotel, to which the party did ample justice. After dinner several drove in waggonettes to Overton, whilst others preferred to ramble by the sea. Tea was partaken ot at the same hotel, and the party reached home about 930. The weather was all that could be wished for, and a most enjoyable day was spent. GOOD TEMPLARY.—ERENEZER LODGE

The Earlestown Ebenezer Lodge held its weekly , session on Tuesday evening in the Co-operative I Hall, Earle-st. Bro. T. Dean, C.T., presided. 'The Secretary gave report of No. 1 Convention held at Hindley. Arrangements were made for an outdoor I meeting on Wednesday evening. One candidate I was duly proposed and admitted to membership. Final arrangements were made for picnic to Frod- sham. Fraternal greetings were received and re- turned to Military Lodge,lndia,and Prescott Lodge, St. Helens. Sigter Hopkins then gave a recitation, Sister Owens a solo, Bro. Dear an address, and Bro. J. Taylor a sole, after which the lodge closed.

div.head: PRESENTATION AT THE VULCAN.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT THE VULCAN.

On Tuesday afternoon at the final meeting of the Session of the Mothers' Sewing meetings held at the Vulcan Feundry Company's Works' dining room, Mrs. Collingwoed and Mrs Norman were each the recipient oE a handsomely bound church service and hymn book at the hands of the mem- bars, in recognition of the interest the two ladies named have shown towards the welfare of the mothers who attend the meetings. The gatherings were organised a few months ago by Mrs. Calling- wood and Mrs. Norman, and a good work has been conducted with much success, and the eff)rts of the organisers have been highly appreciated. it is proposed to start a fresh series of meetings next September. TEMPERANCE PICNIC FROM EARLESTOWN.

The annual picnic in connection with the Cadets of Temperance (Samuel Morley Section) took place on Saturday afternoon under favourable conditions. The party numbering about 160 left Earlestown by the 1.34 train four carriages being reserved for their accommodation. They alighted at Lea Green and marched to Micklahead Green to a &Id placed at their disposal by Mr. G. W. Rawlins, of Rainhill• The day was beautifully fine, and the country round being in excellent condition, the out was much enjoyed. Tte children amused themselves in the field, and about four o'clock tea was served in the schoolroom. The remainder of the evening was spent in games, racing, &c., and the party left ior home about nine o'clock. 11A.YDOCK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCIIOIL.

The annual treat to the scholars attending the above school took place on Saturday afternoon About 360 mustered at the schoolroom at 2.15, and after a procession had been formed they proceeded, headed by the Haydook brass band, to the Heyes where through the kindness of Mrs. Evans, the children were allowed to inspect the gardens, which at the present time are in excellent condition. After leaving the gardens they marched through Hay- dock as far as the Tell Bar and retracing their steps, turned again at the Local Board offices an I afterwards broke up at the schor.l about five o'clock. Tea was served in the schoolroom, and heartily enjoyed by the scholars, their wants being attended to by the teachers. Alter tea the children adjourned to a field behind the school where they amused themselves with games and racing until dusk. The arrangements were in the hands of Mr. W. Briscoe, secretary, and Mr. T. Chalmers, super- intendent. VIADUCT OFFICE STAFF PICNIC.—PRESENTATION
TO MR. ORINIA.ND.

On Saturday the office atall and several of the foremen engaged at the London and North-Western Railway Company Wagon works. Earlestown, had their annual picnic, the destination being B-eston Castle. Thr party left Earlestown at 11.30 for Chester, reaching the ancient city about 1 o'clock Dinner was partaken of at "Ye olde Coach and Horses "Inn, the host, Mr. Barlow, providing an excellent and well served repast. About 2.15, waggonettes were chartered, and the party set eft for Beeston Castle, which was reached shortly after four o'clock. The weather was of a beautiful character, and the country was much admired. The ruins of the old Beeston Castle were inspected, and the view from the heights Was exceptionally fine. For the edification of the visitors, an atteedant lowered a lighted lamp down the Castle well, which is 336 feet deep, and in which at one time it, was supposed a quantity of treasure was buried. Leav- ing the Castle an enjoyable walk through the fields brought the party .to the Beeston Castle Inn, where a substantial tea was provided. After a hearty meal Mr. Reade, on behalf of those present, presented Mr. Ormand with a beautifully chased silver cigarette case, and silver match box, each bearing the monogram" T.O" and "1896." This was sup- plemented by Mr. C. W. Emmett, who moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Ormand for his efforts in con- nection with the annual outin.o, and expressing appreciation for his kindness. Mr. 3. Gooding seconded. Mr. Ormand said he had been in one or two tight corner in his life, but he must candidly confe-s that was the tightest they had put him in that afternoon. Not a word, nor even a whisper of what they intended to do had reached him, conse- quently they would appreciate the surprise, never- theless a pleasurable one, when they called upon Mr. Rea& to speak, and hand him those very hand- some tokens of admiration and regard, (Hear, I hear.) It, was now 10 years ago that, very month since he was asked to take the position of the head of the offi and during the whole of that time he thought he might say he had tried to do his best Iwithout fear or favour, and to serve the interests of the superintendent whom he loved, and those with whom he had worked during that time. (Hear, hear.) He had striven to be somethink more than the head of the office, he had tried to lice in the hearts and aft-ctions of those with whom he came in daily contact. and nothing gave him greater pleasure than to be helpful to those who came to him for advice. Consequently he esteemed that token of their regard anti for the kin lly feelings Which prompted it.fle sincerely hoped that hewever long he might he allowed to preside over that esta- blishment, the same good fellowship might exist. lie thought he should have to ask. them to he satis- fied with asking them to accept his hearty, thanks for the handsome present from the clerks and fore- men sitting roun I that table. It, would he a red letter day in hi: life, and would show him that, he held seme little corner in their hearts. (Applause.) After one or two toasts had been proposed and duly honoured, the party left shortly after s-ven o'clock, and r-ached Earlestown about 11 30, after a most lenioyable outing.

div.head: EXAMINER' SATURDAY, JUNE 27, 1996.
div.p: THE EXAMINER' SATURDAY, JUNE 27, 1996.
WARRINGTOA BOARD OF GUA.RDIANS.

A meeting of this Board was held in the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. G. Pilling occupied the chair, and there were also present, Mrs. Clay, Rev. J. H. Riddette, Dr. Patterson, MPasrs. A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, J. Billinge, G. Thompson, W. Cross, J. Clarke,T. Halton. J. Knowles and J. C. Satton (clerk), S. Sutton (deputy clerk), C. H. Wird (workhouse master), H. M. Mines (superintendent Padgate S3hools), and Jenner-Fust (Local Government Bard ingpector).
A SHALL ATTENDANCE.

The CLERK said the number of Guardians present that morning was smaller than he had known for a long period. The Chairman was absent through sickness in his family, and a number of members were away at Leicester, attending the Royal Agricultural Society's Show.

was entitled to one representative for the district of Littie Sankcy which would be includf- d in the borough. He had pleasure in moving that the Board request the Laucashire County Council to grant that increase.—Mr. Knowles said he was of the opinion that it was decided that the Board did not see tho necessity for any addi- tional guardians.—The Chairman said the subject had been brought forward but no decision was come to.— Mr. Knowles said it was a matter that the Guardians should have had notice of.—The Chairman said he would then give notice that at the next meeting be would bring the matter forward.—The Clerk said the application was necessary in consequence of Little Sankey being included in the borough. Mr. Thompson represented that dis- trict now, and if the application was granted it would not increase the n mber of Guardians.
SLIGGESTIONS BY MIL JENNEB MUST.

Mr. JENNER FUST (Local Government Board inspector) stated that when he attended the Board meeting last year there were three points he directed the members' attention to. The first was that more assistance was required by the Matron ; secondly, the need of more and better accommodation for the sick ; and thirdly,the need of increase in the nursing staff. He was glad to think that since that time the Guardians had given more help to the Matron by the appointment of an as- sistant matron, and had taken an important step to- wards providing better accommodation for the sick by the purchase of additional land and by giving instruc- tions for the preparation of plans for a new Infirmary. He hoped that the sketch plans for the work would soon be submitted to the Local Government Board and that everything would be ready for the reception of patients at the earliest period in the coming year. As regarded the nursing department,the statement he had placed be- fore the members that morning would show how they stood in reference to nurses as compared with other unions in the county. He was rather glad to think that apparently the example set in Lancashire with reference to nurses was to be followed in the country at large, as retures had been asked for dealing with this question. I was another instance of Lancashire taking the lead and the example being fol- lowed throughout the country. They -would see from the return he had made that in January last the Board had two day and one night nurses. That gave them one mare for every 30 patients. The average for the whole of the county was one nurse for every Iff persons. Thus, before they appointed the additional nurse they had in Warrington very little more than half the proportion of nurser in comparison with the number for the county at large. He felt sure that when they got their new in- firmary they would still increase their staff, and he would be glad if they would do so at an early period. There was another paint he ought to call their attention to. In the report al uded to, there was shown for the first time the amount of training which every nurse had had the advantage of. They would see that the three ' nurses employed by that Uniorrhad only had one year's I training. The Guardians should seek to have one or two of their nurses more highly trained. A training of twelve months, however good, was not sufficient to turn out nurses for fulfilling the position of head nurse. He war sorry to say that the return showed an increase of the pauperism of the county a Lancashire as compared with the average for the past five years. The average for the latter period was one pauper for every 57 of the plreilation, but in January last it was one pauper for every 52 Referring to the Warrington Union alone,, the average for the past five years was one for every 57 whilst on the Ist January last it was one for every 49 of the population. If they took the totals, excluding vag- rants (for taking the number of a single night was hardly a fair criterion) the average was 417 indoor paupers in their Union for the past five years as against 527 on the Ist January, and the out- door relief for the same period had increased from 933 recipients to 1,1132 last January, an increase of 229. The Umion's peuneriem at the beginning of the year was therefore 339 in excess of the average for the five preceding yea s. There were only six unions in Ihe county' which had a higher rate of pauperism than Warrington. It was his duty to criticise the condition of the children at Padgate Schools as regarded their personal cleanliness on the last occasion. Mr. Moorsom in his report of an inspection on the 20.:h of last month recorded a great improvement in that respect. An im- portant change had taken place in the management of the Board's schools by the resignation of their superin- tendent, Mr. Mines. Mr. Mines had served as a poor. law officer for a great number of years and they all re- gretted the severe illness which had led to his resigna- tion. Their good wishes followed him in his retirement. Mr. Jenner Fust then proceeded to call the Board's atten- tion to several details in the management. He suggested that the Board should have a foster-mother in each home, and should let the tailor and shoemaker be non- resident officers.—The Chairman thanked Mr. Jenner Fust for his remarks, and stated that the matters he had called their attention to would receive the Board's con- sideration. The Board then rose.

div.head: COST OF A DEPUTATION.
div.p: THE COST OF A DEPUTATION.

The CLERK reprted that the usual charges for the recent deputation from the Board to the Central Poor Law Conferenem at London, of five guineas each had been m ade. This included railway, hotel and cab expenses, &c. At the request of the Registrar General, the depu'ation visited London a day earlier than they otherwise would have done to confer with him on the subject of the registrarship of Latchford, and he (the Clerk) had taken the liberty to charge, subject to the approval of the Board, an extra guinea each.—The expenses were approved of.

div.head: NEW SUPERINTENDENT AND MATRON OF PADGATE
div.p: THE NEW SUPERINTENDENT AND MATRON OF PADGATE
SCHOOLS.

The CLERK read some letters which had been received from Mr. Wright. the newly-appointed superintendent of the above schools, who said he would like to remain at Birkenhead until the 28th July. He and Mrs. Wright would go for a week's holiday on the 25th inst., before commencing their duties at Padgate.—The Rev. J. H. Riddette asked what was the total amount of remunera- tion Mr. and Mrs Wright would receive. He was not aware that any total amount had been stated. It was impossible to ascertain it from the year book, but it was stated in the circular sent to the Guardians that the total amount paid to the outgoing slperintendent and matron was £l6l —The Clerk said the salary as super- intendent was £3O and as schoolmaster £5O. The house, fire, gas. &c., were estimated to be equivalent to £35, and rations at £2B a year. Mr. Wright would not re- ceive whit Mr. Mines now received as bandmaster, namely. £l3 a year. A bandmaster would have to be anpeinted.—The Rev. J. FL Riddette asked if any por- tion of the education erant was transferred to the super- intendent P—The Clerk : Yes, but we don't estimate,that in the amount we pay him!as schoolmaster. It amounts to about £5 a year.—Near the close of the meeting, Mr. Cross asked if it was understood that the new superintendent and matron would receive a pension when they finished their labours at the schools P—Toe Clerk.—They may or may not. That will depend upon the decision of the then Gu Tr) ians. I suggest it is better to let them (Mr. and Mrs. Wright) look after their own interests in that respect. —The subj 'et then drop' ed.

div.head: UNION STATISTICS.
div.p: UNION STATISTICS.

The CLERK reported that the following return had been made in rs.ponse to an application from the Local Government Board. There were 166 adult males receiv- ing nut-door relief within the three relieving districts in the Unnn. None were Army Reserve men, and none Airily Militia men. There was one discharged soldier vrith a nensinn but none without a pension. In compli- ance with an order of the House of Commons, he had prepared a return showing the number of pauper in- mates in the wards for the sick on June Ist together with the numher of those attending to them. On the date named there were in the sick warcls.24 men and 33 women; number of aged, but infirm, 43 men and 100 women •. paid officers as nurses, 3; number of trained rurses,3-; average period of tenure of office, 3 years; number of pauper inmates who assisted in the personal care of the inmates, 7 men and 9 women.

div.head: WALKING DAY..
div.p: WALKING DAY..
It was decided that the scholars of Padgate Schools should have the usual treat on Walk,nz Day and that their railway fares to WArrinarton should be paid.
SUDDEN DF,AT/I OF A BOY.

The CLERK stated that there was rather an unusual report to make with reference to Padgate Schools. A boy named Walter Birchall took ill on 6unday and died during; the night —The Chairman said it was reported that the boy was kicked in the stomach about three years ago. They had had narrow escapes of losing him several times before. The Doctor would not give a cer- tificate of death, and a post mortem examination would be held that day.

div.head: REOISTRATION ARRANGZISIENTS.
div.p: REOISTRATION ARRANGZISIENTS.

The CLERK stated that he received a letter from the Registrar General appointing 2.30 on the 9th inst.l as a suitable day to receive a deputation frc ne the Board with reference to the proposed alterations in the registration arrangements. With regard to this,Mr. Pilling attended with him (the Clerk) at Somerset House and had a long conversation on the question with Mr. Whittaker, who stated that the modern tendency was to limit the number of registration districts where- ever it was practical to do so, ancrthe Regiltrar General thought it might he done in the present else. He (the el.rk) stated that Mr. Pilling was a resident of Latch- ford and connected with the Parish Council of Latch- ford, the portion to be included within the Union, and also that he was a member of the Runcorn Board of Guardians as well as a member of the Warrington Board. He could therefore speak on behalf of the in- habitants and the authorities referred to. A letter had been received by the Superintendent Registrar that morning stating that as the Registrar at the Latchford sub-district desired to be relieved from her duties it was necessary to get someone to act until a decision had been made with regard te the registration arrange ments.—Mr. Pilling moved a resolution that it was de- sirable for the Borough to be formed into two sub- districts for registration purposes, and that one be- formed in that part of the Borough lying south of the river and the other in that portion lying north of the river. He stated that he was well acquainted with the needs of Latchford in the matter, and he thought there should continue to be two sub-districts as had existed since the Union was formed.—Mr. A. Jolley seconded.—Mr. A. J. Jolley said it would be foolish not to support the Registrar's recntnmendation. He would move an amendment that the Board thought it desirable that the registration district should be co-terminus with the municipal borough. It seemed preposterous to maintain a separate registration sub-district because it I had existed previously. The only argument brought forward in support of it at the last meeting was the long distance from the Warrington office, but that was only an argument for putting the Warrington office in a more central situation for the convenience of the inhabitants. It was ridiculous that it should continue in the east end of the town because it had been there for half a century.--N seconder was found for Mr. A. .7. Jollev's amendment, and it therefore fell to the ground. 'fhe resoletion was then carried.—The Chairman moved a further resnlution that Orford should be included in the Winwick registration district in accordance with the Registrar General's recommendation.—This was unanimously agreed to. —The Chairman said they had now to fill temporarily the vacincy of registrar for the Latchford sub-district. He moved that Mr. Frank Auklend, the relieving officer for that district, be the registrar temporarily,and in the event of his permanent appointment he should reside in the district.—Mr. Billinge seconded.—Mr. Knowles thought the relieving officer had enough to attend to with his duties regarding relief without the additional duties of registrar. He proposed that they advertise for a fit and proper porson to carry on the duties of regis- trar. He should strongly object to a relieving officer having an appointment of that kind.—The Chairman said there was no time to advertise for a successor, as the office must be temporarily filled immediately.—Mr. Knowles 54id in that case he would move that the regis- trar appoint a successor.—Mr. Thompson said he agreed with Mr. Knowles. He thought it would be better to let the registrar appoint an officer temporarily. —The Clerk said he had received a letter from the pest master et Latchford applying for the position.—Mr. Jenner Fun asked whether the district would be within the relieving offcer's district. His appointment as re- gistrar would have to receive the sanction of the Local Government Roard fhe Clerk said, he was aware of that. The work would be entirely within his district,and it was a small district.—The Rev. J. H. Riddette said he would like to ask whether it was any advantage that the amalgamation should take place. They would perhaps have to increase their relieving officer's salary if he did not undertake the duties of registrar. In the Newton district the combination of officers had worked admir- ably. He thoueht it was rather an advantage that the two offices should be held by one person.—The Clerk stated that relieving officers were very often appointed registrars. They moved about in the district, and by combining the cluties,a less salary was required than was the case when the offices were separate.—The Chair- man said he would not press his resolution, and would le4ve the matter in the hands of the Registrar General. —The Rev. J. H. Riddette said he hoped the Chairman would go to a vote with his resolution as he heard one Guardian remark that they should tako good care that the resolution was not passed.—Mr. Thompson said he would like to know what Guardian had said that.—The Rev. J. H. Riddette said if they were so particular he would let them know. He did not think there was any- thing wrong in the remark. It was Mr. Thompson.— Mr. Thompson said he did not say so. What he did say was that they must take care the thing was properly gene into.—The Rev. J. B. Riddette: Then I apologise. —Mr. T. Flatten : More ap ,logies. (Laughter.) The sabject then dropped,and the Registrar General will ap- point a successor for the Latchtori sub-district.
THE DEAD EDUCATION BILL.

div.head: NEWTON, 171AYDOCK AND GOLBOR NE BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: NEWTON, 171AYDOCK AND GOLBOR NE BUILDING SOCIETY.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The thirty-sixth annual meeting of the members of this Society was held in the Town Hall. Newton, on Fri- day evening. Mr. J. Sankey presided, and there was a large attendance of shareholders, including Mr. H. J. longton (solicitor), and Mr. J. Adams (secretary).—The Chairman in opening the meeting apologised for the absence of Mr. T. D. Grimke-Drayton who should have presided. but had been called away. The Secretary (Mr. J. Adams) then read the annual repert and statement of accounts which was as under: "The directors have pleasure in reporting to the mem- bers the Society's transactions for the past year, and presenting to them the annexed statement of accounts certified by the auditors. Advances have been made this year on eleven lots of property amounting to £4,830 and after deducting repayments the total sum outstand- ing on properties not in hand is £17,805 133. 7d. on forte-five lots, and the interest received frem them is £833 12s. The profits for the year are £B5B 13s. 7d., and a dividend of five pounds per cent. has been declared which will absorb £Bl4 34. 7d., leaving £44 10s. to be carried to the Contingent Account, which now stands at £2,703 104 6,1. This is over 14 per cent, on the total sum outstanding en mortgage. The Directors congratu- late the members on the continued prosperity of the Society. Advances have been made on a greater num- ber of properties and the amount is largerthan last year; a greater number of invested shares has beenlaken UP ; there is an increase of 20 members for the year; and one property only is in the Sniety's handt. The Direc- tore are prepared to make advances on liberal terms on eligible freehold or leasehold properties, and in addition to the issuing of Invested Shares, they are prepared to receive deposits or loans at a fixed rate of interest of 31 per cent., payable balf-yearly, and sebject to various teems of notice for repayment. The Society consists of 320 members, holding 1,706 invested shares and 2;287 mortgage shares. On toe motion of Mr. E4an,seconded by Dtr. Lawton, the report was adopted. Mr. Longton addressed the meeting briefly, and alluded to the affairs of the society. He thought more. advantage might be taken by the public of the ability of the society to allow 31 per cent. on loans deposited. The security was perfect, as the society could not take any more than a per centage on the amount they had out at mnrtgage.

Mr. J. Sankey was re-elected president., and the retir— ing direct r', Messrs. J. Gibson, S. McDougall, and T. Ritchie were re-sppointed. Mr. A. Rlything was re- elected treasurer, and Messrs. Appleby and Bateman auditors.
A vote of thanks to the :Chairman terminated the meeting.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY. ABANDONMENT OF TETE EDUCATION BILL,

The Flouse having gone into committee on the E luca- tion Bill,Mr. BALFOUR rose and said he had to announce that he should propose that the Chairman leave the chair, a motion which would have the effect of destroy- ing the Bill for the present session. In explanation and justification of the change in the policy of the Govern- ment, he said that under the plan proposed by the Government a week ago 53 days would have been available for the passage of the Bill before financial exi- gencies required or suggested a new session. The op- position they had met with, if continued, would have made 53 days a totally inadequate time for passing the Bill into law. In five days they had only passed two lines and fourteen words of the first clause. The Govern- ment considered they were absolutely pledged to aid the Voluntary schools, and to carry that aid to the furthest extent the Imperial resources would permit. They would take steps to ensure that the Voluntary schools did not suffer by the delay in carrying out their plan. Sir W. FIARCOURT having strongly defended the attitude of the Opposition t mards the Bill, a long discussion followed. The Chairman then left the chair, and the Speaker returned. On the motion of the third reading of the Diseases of Animals Bill, Mr. STUART moved that it be read a third time that day three months. In the course of the de- bate Mr. G. Whiteley (Stockport) said that as an earnest Unionist he was almost heartbroken that in its first seAsion, with a majority of 150, the Government should have devoted almost the whole time of Parliament to measures inimical to the interests of the towns. The motion of the third reading was carried by 232 votes to 75.

In the House of Lords the Earl of DIINRATEN moved the second reading of the Bill for legalising marriage with a deceased wife's sister. He pointed out that in regard to the law of marriage England stood in a posi- tion of isolation—by no means a "splendid " one—as compared with all other civilised countries. Lord PRRCY moved the rejection of the Bill, and was supported by the Archbishop of Canterbury, who said that the Bill would make a ruinous breach in the principle of the marriage law. The Huse divided, and thP second read- ing was carried by Ha votes against 113—a majority of 29. The Prince of Wales and other members of the Royal Family supported the Bill, whi/st twenty prelates voted against It.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Tuesday Mr. MORTON asked the Under Foreign Secretary if he was aware that there were 3,000 Armenians still detained in the prisons of the SultAn. Mr.CuazoN repled that the Government had not recently re,3eived any general report in reference to the number of Armenians detained in Turkish prisons but representations were made to the Turkish Govern- ment whenever cases of hardship and undue detention came to the knowledge of our Embassy in Constanti- nople. _ _ _

Answering Mr. P. Stanhope, Mr. CURZON said steps had already been taken to convey to the President et the French Republic an expression of the high appreciation entertained in this country of the sympathy and admir- able devotion of the officials and population of Ushant and other parts of Brittany in connection with the lamentable wreck of the Drummod Castle.

On the motion that the Agricultural Land Rating Bill as amended in Committee be considered, Mr. J. A. PEASE moved that the relief should be given for tour years only, instead :of five as proposed in the bill. Mr. CHAPLIN refused to accept the amendment. oir W. HAn- couer said the measure:was class legislation of the worst possible character, and the Government ought to oe anxious to shorten the period no that they might make the system, of taxation a fair one. Mr. G. WHITELY (Stockport) pressed the Government ts shorten the period, as he could not but recognize the fact that the boroughs would have a grievance during the currency of the bill, as they would be called on tor five years to not only pay their own heavy rates, but to pay more to reduce the county rate. The amendment was rejected by 258, votes to 140. Mr. SEAL HAYNE then moved that no relief should be given in cases where rents had been raised after the passing of the Act. This was rejected by 216 vote& to 102. Mr. E. Griffith moved that where the landlords paid the rates there should be no deduc- tion from the rates, but this was defeated by 222 to 97.
The Divorce Amendment Bill was read a third time and pxssed in the House of L-,rds yesterday. WEDNESDAY.

The consideration of the Agricultural Land Rating Bill as amended in Committee was continued in the House ot 'ominous on Wednesday, when Mr. KEARLET resumed therdiscussion on Mr. Stuart's amendment to the first clause to tt.e effoct that lan within county or municipal boroughs should not be included isa the opera- tion of the Rat. Eventually Mr. tlatFoutt moved the closure,which was carried by 222 votes to 131., and Mr. Stuart's amendment was defeated by 236. votes to 131. An amenLim.nt moved by Mr. H. LEWIS, that the renal granted should bs one-fourth instead of one-half. was re- jeeted by 234- votes to 116. Mr. Balfour afterwards moved the closure, which was carried by 246 votes to 1.11,a,nd the motion that clause 1 stand part of the Bill was curled by a 43 votes to 134. The House then ad— journed.. THURSDAY.

_ In the House of Commons on Thursday Mr. P. STAN-- HOPE asked whether the Government had received any coufirmatiJon of the terrible reports appearing in the papers as to the operations of the Turkish troops in Crete. Mr. Curzon replied that tbe reports from the Consul at Crete gave a general confirmation of the-state- ments that had appeared. The representatives of the six Powers, who were acting in entire accord, had made representations to the Porte with regard to the measures necessary for he restoration of order.

Mr. Eiunasked whether ia;i:ci--i;lisbury's attention had been called to the report of the Commissioner of the Armenian, Relief Fund respecting his visit to the pro- vince ot Kliarput, and the terrible devastation of that province by fire and sword. Mr. CURZON said attention nad been directed to the report, and "strong represen- tations" had been made to the Turkish Government. Mr., ELLis asked whether the Government intenJed to do nothing more than make these "strong re- presentations." Mr. Ghazni.; replied that the Govern- ment must wait and see what weight those representa- tions had..

Sir W. HARCOURT asked when the searching inquiry into toe origin and circumstances of the invasion ot the Transvaal by forces under the control ,of the Chartered Company was t 3 be instituted. Mr. LHAMMIRLAIN re- plied that the House was aware that the Government had promised t') make proposals for a further inquiry to the House as soon as the trial of Dr. Jameson was concluded.
The consideration of the Agricultural Land Rating Bill as•atmended in Committee was resumed. A number of amendments were disposed of, and clause 4 was then considered.
