div.p: WARRINGTON.
WITNFRAL OF THE. • LiTE LORD LILFORIN

The funeral of the late Lord Lilford took-pce on Saturday afternoon at Thorpe Achurch, Northamp- tonshire. The service was conducted by the Bishop and the Rev. F. G. andgson,rector of Peterborough, the Rev. C. E. Weston, rector of The mourners included Lady Lil- Tofocb oAdr,i pd.l\ Mr. ncjkholuhern. c haT.nd r Powye (the new peer and peeress), Mr. Stephen Powys (son pf the deceased), the R-tv. E. V. R. Powys (brother), Miss Baillie ly'amiiton (sister to Lady Lilford), the Marquess of Exeter, Viscount Melville, Mr. W. W. Dundas, Sir Herewald Wake, and Dean Ingram.—Before com- mencing his sermon at the Warrington Parish Church, on Sunday morning, the Rev. A. A. Mark- ham, referring the late Lord Lilford, said he was ' the patron of the living,and seemed to have realised to the full the responsibility of that position. With ' regard to the parish and all its institutions he seemed to have taken a very clear interest, as well as in the Training College, the Clergy Daughters' School, and the Grammar School. But for many years past, as they knew, he had been a great sufferer, an.d though he had wished to come to Warrington, and to personally see the good works he had always interested himself in, he hod not of late been able to do so. For one like :Lord Lilford, who in his high position realised the duties en- trusted to hitn„and :-eemed to have set to all a lofty ex.imple of a high-minded Christian gentleman, be thought that as a congregation they could not be too thankful. And while they felt that by his death they had lost a true friend, they would not be behindhand in expressing sympathy for those who f.lt the loss more keenly—the family which had been bereaved by his death.

€IIARGR aPSTEALING WHISKY AT GRAPPENHALL. At the Warrington Occasional Court on Tue-day before Mr. Harrison Tinsley, a farm labourer,named Thomas Stanton who had been employed at Grap- penhall was charged with stealing one pint of whisky. value 24., the property of John Thomas, at Grappenhall, on the 22nd inst.—Mrs. Thomas, wife of the complainant, who is licensee of the Rams Read, Orappenhall, stated that the prisoner came to the house about eight o'clock the previous morning! and called for a pint of beer. He was then per- fectly sober and she served him with the beer. Some time afterwards, she heard the prisoner sing- ing and on going into the room she saw that he was in a state of intoxication. She Sent for her husband who on examining the cup from which the prisoner had been drinking found it half full of raw whisky. On ex,imining the whisky utensils it was found that one had been tampered with. Information was then given to the police who took the prisoner into custody. Sufficient evidence having been given to justify a remand the prisoner was according!y remanded until the next Daresbury Petty Sessions

div.head: NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.
At Halifax on Saturday a man named Drinkwater, of Brand %, Hole, was fined for drunkenness.

There was not such an improvement in the shipping t ade of this country as was expected in 1895 over 1894. Indeed, there was a slight falling off both in the number and the tonnage of British vessels and of foreign vessels entered and cleared, though there was a considerable improvement in the figures of 1894. over those of 1893. The falling off, however, in 1895 seems to have been mainly in the coasting trade,for the foreign trade shows a small increase.

The Earl of Crewe opened a new Liberal Club at Corn- holme,in the Sowerby Division, on Saturday. Speaking at a meeting in the evening held at Todmorden, Lord Crewe made a good pilot against the Government when he said its policy in regard to to the Education Bill seemed like the advance of troops along the Nile—its ad- vance being dependent upon the resistance it met with. Mr. Schwann, M.P., said that if the Bill were dropped the verdict would be" Died by the visitation of Pro- vidence,bnt under very suspicious circumstances." Mr. Mellor said the withdrawal of tly3 Bill would be "a tre- mendous confession of failure."

In army circles there is a good deal of adverse critic- ism regarding the granting of" a bloodless medal" to those who took part in the Ashantee expedition. The march to Cuornassi was not one of any particular diffi- culty,and certainly not a dangerous one in the usual ac- ceptation of the term. To grant a medal for such a campaign when no such award was made to the men of Sir Charles Warren's Bechuanaland fighting force is thought to be bringing medals and decorations into con- tempt.

The report of the Registrar of Friendly Societies for 1895 states that 1,067 new societies or branches were reg- istered during the ye r.including 875 friendly societies, 67 trades unions, and 46 building societies. The new friendly societies registered increased by 31, wolking- men's clubs 6, specially authorised societies 14, and loan societies one, while there was a decrease of 29 in the nunsher of new indusl fiat and provident societies regis- tered, 25 in new buiiding societies, one in new trades unions, and two in scientific and literary societies.

The Manchester Corporation is making a desperate attempt to restrict the right of free speech in its parks. For some years the local Fabians have held meetings in Boggart Hole Clough,and while this open space remained private prop4rty they were undisturbed. Last year it was bought by the corporation as a public park. For a time meetings were sanctioned, but during the last few weeks an attempt has been made to suppress them. The reason given is that the avenues are obstructed, and dis- turbances created. Until the corporation adopted its present procedure the meetings of the Sunday Independ- ent Labour party only attracted a few hundreds at most and were held in a gully. Now over ten thousand per- sons attend every Sunday meeting, and the corperatinn is doing its beat by its short sighted policy to increase the crowd and to win recruits for the party. A number of speakers have been fined, others have been bound over "to keep the peace," including the Hon. Roden Noel, while Mr. Leonard Hall and Mr. Fred Brocklehurst, well known local labour leaders, are serving a month's imprisonment, having refused to pay the fines imposed.

Sunday was an interesting day for London Noncon- formists. The new Presbyterian Church at Altenburg- gardens, in Clapham. was used for ordinary Sunday ser- vices for the first time, whilst at the Congregational Church in Grafton-square, the first two of a series of special services were held to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the introduction of Congregationalism into the parish. the Rev. Morlais Jones, chairman of the Congregational Union, preached in the morning, and the Rev. Dr. Richardson, of Nashua, New Hampshire, 117. S A., in the evening. The founder of the Dissenting community in Clapham was the Rev. William Bridge, M A.,.rf Cambridge University,one of the five independ- ent ministers in the Assembly of Divines at Westminster. Having laN3n silenced by Bishon Wren in 1637, he with- drew to Holland, but about 1640 returned to England, and commenced preaching on his own account in a wooden building in what •is now North-street, but was then known as Nag's Head-lane. The work which he commenced has been continued uninterruptedly by a succession of distinguished tninisters,the latest being the Rev. Dr. Guinness Rogers, who has held the pastorate since 1665.

Mr. E. Dicey,writinF.; to`the "London Observer" on the Thant shipwreck, relates an experience which he timl in passing this dangerous corner in a Union liner six years ago. Save that the time WAS afternoon, the cir- cumstances of the incident were much the same as in the rasa of the Drummond Castle. There was a perfectly riem sea and a white fog. On the fog lifting a cry of " Whales !" was raised. These " whales" were the hacks of the same black rocks between Ushant and Mile Won which the Drummond Castle ran, but which in the earlier case, thanks to the lifting of the fog and to skilful seamanship, were narrowly avoided. One of the .ffieers assured him that according to all calcula- tions the r mks in question ought to have lain ten miles to the right, and 'hat the disturbing element must have been a strong current running towards the shore. It must remain a question for navigators whether the usual three miles is en nigh berth to give to such a dangerous spot as irshant. Given a foggy night and a deflexion of half a point from the course owing to the current, a disaster is almost unavoidabte,unless,indeed,the steamer is brought to a full stop, which is the rule with the beats from LP Conquet to Ushant.

At the Firemen's Tournament,London,on Monday after- noon much interest was taken in the display of the Cana- dian extension ladder by men of the Montreal fire bri- gade. This ingenious piece of mechanism, which owes its origin to /VI. Collerette (who is himself a fireman),may b. described Rs a folding staircase carried on a four-wheel drat of enormous length, and reaching when extended to its fullest dimensions the height of 114 feet, or 24 feet in excess of the longest fire-ladders used in the United States. The ladder, when raised to the required altitude is made to revolve on a pivot, and is easily adjusted tO difficu!t situations and awkward angles. At the tourna- ment therhose reel was used in conjunction with it,won- derful skill and dash being displayed by the Transatlan- tic firenaon. The hose, payed out while the car was drlven at full gallop, was drawn in an incredibly short time to the ton rf the ladder. Immediately afterwards the London firemen showed that they were not to be outdone in nimbleness, and though their machinery was much tn,rre primitive than that of their Canadian rivals I the Londoners proved themselves quite as smart and speedy in their work. Truth to tell, the Canadian lad- der would not be easy to work in the narrow streets on acroant of the great length of the car on which it has to he borne. There seems to be no reason, however, why the hose reel should not have a trial in this country.

The grand kiry have found a true bill against Dr Jameson and the other defendants, and their trial will soon be proceoded with, and the ground will be cleared for the bigger criestions that lie beyond. The sty to follow the finding of the true bill will be the demand of the irtorney-General that the prisoners be tried at Bar. There is no power m the court to refuse this demand, and in the present instance there will be no inclination, even if there were the power. This form of trial secures the presence of three judges on the bench, and it is a right reserved to the Crown in cases where its authority is concerned. It is a privilege that is rarely exercised, the last of the kind having been the notorious fichbr)tirne trial. There seems to be no doubt that the Lord Chief Justice will preside, and gossip is busy with the names of the others. Probably it is right in fixing on Mr. Justice Hawkins as one, but several are spoken of as the probable third. There is no reason to b-lieve that the proceedings will be protracted—at least Sir Edward Ctark—'s hint that the defence would be chiefly legal and constitutional may allow of the case being dis- posed of in less than a week.

The death of Sir Augustus Harris has produced wide- spread regret in many circles. Perhaps there has never been a m re popular manager connected with the Brit- ish stage, unless indeed it was his father, and it would hardly be possible to find one with more energy and initiative. He seems to have been born with a genuis for theatrical management ; and the rapidity with avhici he shot into a position of responsibility was an indica- tion of the ereat administrative powers which he was subsequently to exhibit in a wide field. The stage pro- per does not owe nearly so much to him as does the opera. At a moment when Italian opera seemed to have become extinct he gave it a new period of life and popu- larity. English opera also has passed into a new stage r,f revival in London under him. Pantomime owes as much to him as does the opera, and in his hands it has entered upon fresh developments. For his new form of pantomime he had to create a school for the teaching of ballet dancing. Etc did not touch, however, the higher field of dramatic art. That he left to such men as Sir H. Irvine. But his energy and grasp of details were unbounded ; and half a dozen prosperous enterprises will now be in want of a guiding hand.

_ In the House of Cc mmons on Monday night leave was given to bring in a Bill to confirm a provi- sional order of the Local Government Board relat- ing to Warrington. The Bill is to enable the Cor- poration to amend the local Acts, increasing their borrowing power., and to regulate the line of buildings end other matters. Tlll4 WARRINGTON VOLUNTRERS.

The annual inspection ball of the Ist V.8.P.(W.V)., was held on Monday night in the Drill hail, and was a great success. There was a large attendance, which included a number of sergeants and their wives 'from Orford Barracks and several from the Newton Company. Dancing commenced at nine o'clock,and was kept up with spirit until about one o clock on the following morning;to music supplied ,by the regimental band under the direction of Bandmaster T. Armstrong. Light refreshments were I supplied by Quartermaster-Sergeant A. Potter.
